cbv4:1.1.1.verse: There are in this body: hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spit, mucus, synovic fluid, urine, and the brain in the head.

“In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.”

cbv5:1.1.1.verse: With proper discernment I make use of the robe,

cbv5:1.1.2.verse: only to ward off the cold, to ward off the heat, to ward off contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, the heat (of the sun), and creeping things, only as a cover for the shameful parts.

cbv5:1.1.3.verse: With proper discernment I make use of almsfood,

cbv5:1.1.4.verse: not for sport, or for showing off, not for ornament, or for adornment, but only to maintain this body, and to carry on, to inhibit annoyance, and to assist in the spiritual life, and so I will get rid of any old feeling, and not produce any new feeling, and there will be support for me, being blameless, and living comfortably.

cbv5:1.1.5.verse: With proper discernment I make use of a dwelling,

cbv5:1.1.6.verse: only to ward off the cold, to ward off the heat, to ward off contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, the heat (of the sun), and serpents, only to dispel the trouble of the (varying) seasons, and so as to delight in seclusion.

cbv5:1.1.7.verse: With proper discernment I make use of the requisite of medicine for support when sick,

cbv5:1.1.8.verse: only to ward off oppressive feelings that have arisen and at least be free from oppression.

cbv5:1.1.1.verse: Take a mendicant who, reflecting rationally, makes use of robes:

cbv5:1.1.2.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; and for covering up the private parts.’

cbv5:1.1.3.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of almsfood:

cbv5:1.1.4.verse: ‘Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support spiritual practice. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will have the means to keep going, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding.’

cbv5:1.1.5.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of lodgings:

cbv5:1.1.6.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off cold and heat; for warding off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; to shelter from harsh weather and to enjoy retreat.’

cbv5:1.1.7.verse: Reflecting rationally, they make use of medicines and supplies for the sick:

cbv5:1.1.8.verse: ‘Only for the sake of warding off the pains of illness and to promote good health.’

cbv6:0.1.verse: The Discourse on the Ten Things

cbv6:2.1.verse: This is what the Great Sage preached about the qualities of the monks,

cbv6:3.1.verse: after hearing it, and while practising, he is freed from all suffering.

cbv6:4.1.verse: For the whole world’s benefit and welfare we will recite that safeguard.

cbv6:7.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī

cbv6:8.1.verse: at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv6:9.1.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

cbv6:10.1.verse: “Monks!”, “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

cbv6:11.1.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

cbv6:12.1.1.verse: “There are these ten things, monks, that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on.

cbv6:12.1.3.verse: “I have become one who has no (distinctive) appearance”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.4.verse: “I am bound to others for my livelihood”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.5.verse: “I should comport myself differently”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.6.verse: “Can I myself find no fault with my virtue?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.7.verse: “Will my wise companions in the spiritual life, after testing me, find no fault with my virtue?”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.8.verse: “There is alteration in, and separation from, all that is dear and appealing to me”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.9.verse: “It is actions that I own, it is actions that I am heir to, it is actions that I am born from, actions are my kinsfolk, actions are my refuge -

cbv6:12.1.10.verse: whatever actions I perform, whether good or bad, to that I will be the heir”, one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.11.verse: “In what way do the nights and days pass for me?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.12.verse: “Do I delight in empty places?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.13.verse: “Has a state beyond (ordinary) human beings - the distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and seeing - been attained by me? ° Will I at the end, when questioned by my companions in the spiritual life, not be embarrassed?” one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on this.

cbv6:12.1.14.verse: These are the ten things, monks, that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect on.”

cbv6:25.2.verse: and those monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in the Fortunate One’s words.

cbv6:12.1.1.verse: “Mendicants, one who has gone forth should often review these ten things.

cbv6:12.1.3.verse: One who has gone forth should often review this: ‘I have secured freedom from class.’

cbv6:12.1.4.verse: ‘My livelihood is tied up with others.’

cbv6:12.1.6.verse: ‘I hope there’s no reason to blame myself when it comes to ethical conduct?’

cbv6:12.1.7.verse: ‘I hope that, after examination, sensible spiritual companions don’t reproach any aspect of my ethics?’

cbv6:12.1.8.verse: ‘I must be parted and separated from all I hold dear and beloved.’

cbv6:12.1.9.verse: ‘I am the owner of my deeds and heir to my deeds. Deeds are my womb, my relative, and my refuge.

cbv6:12.1.10.verse: I shall be the heir of whatever deeds I do, whether good or bad.’

cbv6:12.1.11.verse: ‘As the days and nights pass by, what sort of person am I becoming?’

cbv6:12.1.12.verse: ‘Do I love to stay in empty huts?’

cbv6:12.1.13.verse: ‘Do I have any superhuman distinctions in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, so that when my spiritual companions question me on my deathbed I will not be embarrassed?’

cbv6:12.1.14.verse: One who has gone forth should often review these ten things.”

cbv10:5.1.1.verse: At one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv10:5.1.2.verse: Then at that time near Sāvatthī a certain monk was bitten by a snake and died.

cbv10:5.1.3.verse: Then a great many monks approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, they sat down on one side. While sitting on one side those monks said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv10:5.1.4.verse: “Here, reverend Sir, near Sāvatthī, a certain monk has been bitten by a snake and has died”.

cbv10:5.1.5.verse: “Surely, monks, that monk did not suffuse the four royal families of snakes with a mind (full of) friendliness.

cbv10:5.1.6.verse: For if, monks, that monk had suffused the four royal families of snakes with a mind (full of) friendliness then that monk, monks, would not have been bitten by a snake and died.

cbv10:5.1.7.verse: Who are the four royal families of snakes?

cbv10:5.1.8.verse: The Virūpakkha royal family of snakes, the Erāpatha royal family of snakes, the Chabyāputta royal family of snakes, the Kaṇhāgotamaka royal family of snakes.

cbv10:5.1.9.verse: Surely, monks, that monk did not suffuse these four royal families of snakes with a mind (full of) friendliness.

cbv10:5.1.10.verse: For if, monks, that monk had suffused these four royal families of snakes with a mind (full of) friendliness, then that monk, monks, would not have been bitten by a snake and died.

cbv10:5.1.11.verse: I allow you, monks, to suffuse these four royal families of snakes with a mind (full of) friendliness, to guard yourselves, to protect yourselves, to safeguard yourselves.”

cbv10:5.1.12.verse: I am friendly with the Virūpakkhas,

cbv10:5.1.13.verse: with the Erāpathas I am friendly,

cbv10:5.1.14.verse: I am friendly with the Chabyāputtas,

cbv10:5.1.16.verse: I am friendly with those without feet,

cbv10:5.1.17.verse: with those with two feet I am friendly,

cbv10:5.1.18.verse: I am friendly with those with four feet,

cbv10:5.1.19.verse: with those with many feet I am friendly.

cbv10:5.1.20.verse: May the one without feet not hurt me,

cbv10:5.1.21.verse: may the one with two feet not hurt me,

cbv10:5.1.22.verse: may the one with four feet not hurt me,

cbv10:5.1.23.verse: may the one with many feet not hurt me.

cbv10:5.1.24.verse: May all beings, all living creatures,

cbv10:5.1.25.verse: all who are born, in their entirety,

cbv10:5.1.27.verse: may nothing bad come to anyone.

cbv10:5.1.34.verse: I have made this protection, I have made this safeguard,

cbv10:5.1.37.verse: I revere the seven Perfect Sambuddhas.”

cbv10:5.1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

cbv10:5.1.2.verse: Now, at that time a monk in Sāvatthī passed away due to a snake bite.

cbv10:5.1.3.verse: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

cbv10:5.1.4.verse: “Sir, a monk in Sāvatthī has passed away due to a snake bite.”

cbv10:5.1.5.verse: “Mendicants, that monk mustn’t have spread a mind of love to the four royal snake families.

cbv10:5.1.6.verse: If he had, he wouldn’t have died due to a snake bite.

cbv10:5.1.8.verse: The royal snake families of Virūpakkha, Erāpatha, Chabyāputta, and Kaṇhāgotamaka. …

cbv10:5.1.11.verse: Mendicants, I urge you to spread a mind of love to the four royal snake families, for your own safety, security, and protection.

cbv10:5.1.20.verse: May the footless not harm me!

cbv10:5.1.21.verse: May I not be harmed by the two-footed!

cbv10:5.1.22.verse: May the four-footed not harm me!

cbv10:5.1.23.verse: May I not be harmed by the many-footed!

cbv10:5.1.24.verse: All sentient beings, all living things,

cbv10:5.1.26.verse: may they see only nice things,

cbv10:5.1.27.verse: may bad not come to anyone.

cbv10:5.1.34.verse: I’ve made this safeguard, I’ve made this protection:

cbv10:5.1.36.verse: And so I revere the Blessed One,

cbv10:5.1.37.verse: I revere the seven perfectly awakened Buddhas.”

cbv11:5.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī

cbv11:5.2.verse: at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv11:6.1.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

cbv11:7.1.verse: “Monks!”, “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

cbv11:8.1.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

cbv11:9.1.1.verse: “Monks, from the freedom of mind by friendliness meditation, when practised, developed, made much of, carried on, established, maintained, augmented, and properly instigated, eleven advantages are to be expected.

cbv11:9.1.3.verse: He sleeps happily, he wakes up happily, he does not see bad dreams, he is dear to human beings, he is dear to non-human beings, the gods protect him, neither fire, poison, or sword can affect him, he can concentrate his mind quickly, his complexion becomes clear, he dies unbewildered, and if he penetrates no further, he will (at least) go to the Brahma world.

cbv11:9.1.4.verse: Monks, from the freedom of mind by friendliness meditation, when practised, developed, made much of, carried on, established, maintained, augmented, and properly instigated, there are these eleven advantages to be expected.”

cbv11:10.2.verse: and those monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in the Fortunate One’s words.

cbv11:9.1.1.verse: “Mendicants, you can expect eleven benefits when the heart’s release by love has been cultivated, developed, and practiced, made a vehicle and a basis, kept up, consolidated, and properly implemented.

cbv11:9.1.3.verse: You sleep at ease. You wake happily. You don’t have bad dreams. Humans love you. Non-humans love you. Deities protect you. You can’t be harmed by fire, poison, or blade. Your mind quickly enters immersion. Your face is clear and bright. You don’t feel lost when you die. If you don’t penetrate any higher, you’ll be reborn in a realm of divinity.

cbv11:9.1.4.verse: You can expect eleven benefits when the heart’s release by love has been cultivated, developed, and practiced, made a vehicle and a basis, kept up, consolidated, and properly implemented.”

cbv14:6.1.7.verse: Then, referring to the young deva Candimā, the Blessed One addressed Rāhu, lord of the asuras, in verse:

cbv14:6.1.11.verse: Buddhas have compassion for the world.”

cbv14:6.1.12.verse: Then Rāhu, lord of the asuras, released the young deva Candimā and hurriedly approached Vepacitti, lord of the asuras.  Having approached, shocked and terrified, he stood to one side.

cbv14:6.1.13.verse: Then, as he stood there, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, addressed him in verse:

cbv14:6.1.14.verse: “Why, Rāhu, did you come in a hurry?

cbv14:6.1.16.verse: Having come as if in shock,

cbv14:6.1.17.verse: Why do you stand there frightened?”

cbv14:6.1.18.verse: “My head would have split in seven parts,

cbv14:6.1.19.verse: While living I would have found no ease,

cbv14:6.1.20.verse: If, when chanted over by the Buddha’s verse,

cbv14:6.1.21.verse: I had not let go of Candimā. ”

cbv15:2.1.verse: The Sun, who was seized by Rāhu, was released by that (safeguard’s) power,

cbv15:2.2.verse: the destruction of fear of all foes we will recite that safeguard.

cbv15:5.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī

cbv15:5.2.verse: at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv15:6.1.1.verse: Then at that time the Sun god was seized by the asura lord Rāhu.

cbv15:6.1.2.verse: Then the Sun god, recollecting the Fortunate One, on that occasion recited this verse:

cbv15:6.1.4.verse: you who are free in every way!

cbv15:6.1.6.verse: therefore please be a refuge to me.”

cbv15:6.1.7.verse: Then, with reference to the Sun god, the Fortunate One addressed the asura lord Rāhu with a verse:

cbv15:6.1.8.verse: “To the Realised One, the Worthy One,

cbv15:6.1.9.verse: the Sun has gone for refuge,

cbv15:6.1.10.verse: you must release the Sun, Rāhu!

cbv15:6.1.12.verse: He who, in complete darkness, is a light-maker,

cbv15:6.1.13.verse: who is brilliant, a great circle of fire,

cbv15:6.1.14.verse: do not devour he who roams the sky, Rāhu!

cbv15:6.1.15.verse: Release the Sun, who is my kinsman, Rāhu!”

cbv15:6.1.16.verse: Then the asura lord Rāhu, having released the Sun god, hurriedly approached the asura lord Vepacitti, and after approaching, anxious, and horrified, he stood on one side.

cbv15:6.1.17.verse: While he was standing on one side the asura lord Vepacitti recited this verse to the asura lord Rāhu:

cbv15:6.1.21.verse: why do you stand (there) like someone anxious and frightened?”

cbv15:6.1.23.verse: while living I will have no happiness,

cbv15:6.1.24.verse: - I am one to whom the Buddha has chanted a verse

cbv15:6.1.25.verse: if I do not release the Sun.”

cbv15:6.1.1.verse: Now at that time the Sun God had been seized by Rāhu, lord of titans.

cbv15:6.1.2.verse: Then the Sun God, recollecting the Buddha, at that time spoke this verse:

cbv15:6.1.7.verse: Then the Buddha addressed Rāhu in verse concerning the Sun God:

cbv15:6.1.8.verse: “The Sun God has gone for refuge

cbv15:6.1.9.verse: to the Realized One, the perfected one.

cbv15:6.1.10.verse: The Buddhas have compassion for the world—

cbv15:6.1.12.verse: He is a beacon in the darkness,

cbv15:6.1.13.verse: the dazzling sun, circle of awesome might.

cbv15:6.1.14.verse: Rāhu, do not swallow him as he traverses the sky.

cbv15:6.1.15.verse: Rāhu, release my offspring, the Sun!”

cbv15:6.1.16.verse: Then Rāhu, having released the Sun, rushed to see Vepacitti, lord of titans and stood to one side, shocked and awestruck.

cbv15:6.1.20.verse: and came here looking like you’re in shock:

cbv15:6.1.21.verse: why do you stand there so scared?”

cbv15:6.1.22.verse: “My head would have exploded in seven pieces,

cbv15:6.1.23.verse: I would have found no joy in life,

cbv15:6.1.24.verse: if, when enchanted by the Buddha’s verse,

cbv15:6.1.25.verse: I had not released the Sun.”

cbv15:6.1.1.verse: Now on that occasion the young deva Suriya had been seized by Rāhu, lord of the asuras.

cbv15:6.1.2.verse: Then, recollecting the Blessed One, the young deva Suriya on that occasion recited this verse:

cbv15:6.1.3.verse: “Let homage be to you, the Buddha!

cbv15:6.1.4.verse: O hero, you are everywhere released.

cbv15:6.1.7.verse: Then, referring to the young deva Suriya, the Blessed One addressed Rāhu, lord of the asuras, in verse:

cbv15:6.1.11.verse: Buddhas have compassion for the world.

cbv15:6.1.13.verse: The disk of fiery might in the gloom,

cbv15:6.1.14.verse: O Rāhu, do not swallow the radiant one, while (it's) moving across the sky

cbv15:6.1.16.verse: Then Rāhu, lord of the asuras, released the young deva Suriya and hurriedly approached Vepacitti, lord of the asuras. Having approached, shocked and terrified, he stood to one side.

cbv15:6.1.17.verse: Then, as he stood there, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, addressed him in verse:

cbv15:6.1.18.verse: “Why, Rāhu, did you come in a hurry?

cbv15:6.1.20.verse: Having come as if in shock,

cbv15:6.1.21.verse: Why do you stand there frightened?”

cbv15:6.1.22.verse: “My head would have split in seven parts,

cbv15:6.1.23.verse: While living I would have found no ease,

cbv15:6.1.24.verse: If, when chanted over by the Buddha’s verses,

cbv15:6.1.25.verse: I had not let go of Suriya.”

cbv16:0.1.verse: Safeguard through the Top of a Banner

cbv16:2.1.verse: By the recollection of that (safeguard) living creatures in the firmament

cbv16:2.2.verse: obtain complete support, just like (living creatures) everywhere on earth.

cbv16:2.3.verse: From the net of all adversity arising from yakkhas, thieves, and rivals,

cbv16:2.4.verse: those who were released cannot be numbered, we will recite that safeguard.

cbv16:5.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī

cbv16:5.2.verse: at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv16:6.1.1.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

cbv16:6.1.3.verse: “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

cbv16:6.1.4.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

cbv16:6.1.5.verse: “Formerly, monks, there was a massed battle between the gods and the asuras.

cbv16:6.1.6.verse: Then, monks, the lord of the gods Sakka addressed the Tāvatiṁsa gods, saying:

cbv16:6.1.7.verse: ‘If, dear Sirs, to the gods who have gone into battle there should arise fear, or terror, or horror, at that time you could look for the top of my banner.

cbv16:6.1.8.verse: For to those who look to the top of my banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.9.verse: If you cannot look to the top of my banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner.

cbv16:6.1.10.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.11.verse: If you cannot look to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner.

cbv16:6.1.12.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.13.verse: If you cannot look to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner, then you could look for the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner.

cbv16:6.1.14.verse: For to those who look to the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.’

cbv16:6.1.15.verse: But, monks, to he who looks to the top of the lord of the gods Sakka’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Pajāpati’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Varuṇa’s banner, or who looks to the top of the god-king Īsāna’s banner, whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, may be given up, and may not be given up.

cbv16:6.1.16.verse: What is the reason for that?

cbv16:6.1.17.verse: The lord of the gods Sakka, monks, is not free from passion, is not free from hatred, is not free from delusion, being fearful, terrified, scared, he ran away.

cbv16:6.1.19.verse: ‘If to you, monks, after going to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, there should arise fear, or terror, or horror, at that time you could recollect me thus:

cbv16:6.1.20.verse: “Such is he, the Fortunate One, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, the one endowed with understanding and good conduct, the Happy One, the One who understands the worlds, the unsurpassed guide for those people who need taming, the Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Fortunate One.”

cbv16:6.1.21.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect me whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.22.verse: If you cannot recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma thus:

cbv16:6.1.23.verse: “The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Fortunate One, it is visible, not subject to time, inviting inspection, onward leading, and can be understood by the wise for themselves.”

cbv16:6.1.24.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect the Dhamma whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.25.verse: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Saṅgha thus:

cbv16:6.1.26.verse: “The Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are good in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are upright in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are systematic in their practice, the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples are correct in their practice, that is to say, the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons, this is the Fortunate One’s Saṅgha of disciples, they are worthy of offerings, of hospitality, of gifts, and of reverential salutation, they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”

cbv16:6.1.27.verse: For, monks, to those who recollect the Saṅgha whatever fear there may be, or terror, or horror, will be given up.

cbv16:6.1.28.verse: What is the reason for that?

cbv16:6.1.29.verse: The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, is free from passion, is free from hatred, is free from delusion, not being fearful, not terrified, not scared, he did not run away.’”

cbv16:6.1.31.verse: and after saying this, the Happy One, the Teacher, said something more:

cbv16:6.1.32.verse: “In the wilds, at the root of a tree,

cbv16:6.1.33.verse: or in an empty place, monks,

cbv16:6.1.35.verse: and there will be no fear for you.

cbv16:6.1.36.verse: if you can’t remember the Buddha,

cbv16:6.1.38.verse: then you must remember the Dhamma,

cbv16:6.1.39.verse: which leads out, which is well preached.

cbv16:6.1.40.verse: If you can’t remember the Dhamma,

cbv16:6.1.41.verse: which leads out, which is well preached,

cbv16:6.1.42.verse: then you must remember the Saṅgha,

cbv16:6.1.43.verse: which is an unsurpassed field of merit.

cbv16:6.1.44.verse: Thus for those who remember the Buddha,

cbv16:6.1.45.verse: the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, monks,

cbv16:6.1.46.verse: (there will be no) fear, or terror,

cbv16:6.1.1.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

cbv16:6.1.5.verse: “Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the titans.

cbv16:6.1.6.verse: Then Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the gods of the thirty-three:

cbv16:6.1.7.verse: ‘Good fellows, when the gods are fighting, if you get scared or terrified, just look up at my banner’s crest.

cbv16:6.1.8.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.9.verse: If you can’t see my banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of the Progenitor, king of gods.

cbv16:6.1.10.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.11.verse: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Varuṇa, king of gods.

cbv16:6.1.12.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.13.verse: If you can’t see his banner’s crest, then look up at the banner’s crest of Īsāna, king of gods.

cbv16:6.1.14.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.’

cbv16:6.1.15.verse: However, when they look up at those banner’s crests their fear and terror might go away or it might not.

cbv16:6.1.17.verse: Because Sakka is not free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearful, scared, nervous, quick to flee.

cbv16:6.1.19.verse: If you’ve gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and you get scared or terrified, just recollect me:

cbv16:6.1.20.verse: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

cbv16:6.1.21.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.22.verse: If you can’t recollect me, then recollect the teaching:

cbv16:6.1.23.verse: ‘The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.’

cbv16:6.1.24.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.25.verse: If you can’t recollect the teaching, then recollect the Saṅgha:

cbv16:6.1.26.verse: ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples is practicing the way that’s good, direct, systematic, and proper. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.’

cbv16:6.1.27.verse: Then your fear and terror will go away.

cbv16:6.1.29.verse: Because the Realized One is free of greed, hate, and delusion. He is fearless, brave, bold, and stands his ground.”

cbv16:6.1.30.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

cbv16:6.1.31.verse: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

cbv16:6.1.32.verse: “In the wilderness, at a tree’s root,

cbv16:6.1.33.verse: or an empty hut, O mendicants,

cbv16:6.1.35.verse: and no fear will come to you.

cbv16:6.1.36.verse: If you can’t recollect the Buddha—

cbv16:6.1.37.verse: the eldest in the world, the captain of men—

cbv16:6.1.40.verse: If you can’t recollect the teaching—

cbv16:6.1.45.verse: the teaching, and the Saṅgha, mendicants,

cbv16:6.1.47.verse: and goosebumps will be no more.”

cbv16:6.1.1.verse: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:

cbv16:6.1.5.verse: “Bhikkhus, once in the past the devas and the asuras were arrayed for battle.

cbv16:6.1.6.verse: Then Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tavatimsa devas thus:

cbv16:6.1.7.verse: ‘Dear sirs, when the devas are engaged in battle, if fear or trepidation or terror should arise, on that occasion you should look up at the crest of my standard.

cbv16:6.1.8.verse: For when you look up at the crest of my standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.9.verse: If you cannot look up at the crest of my standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Pajapati's standard. For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.10.verse: If you cannot look up at the crest of the deva-king Pajapati's standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Varuna's standard.

cbv16:6.1.11.verse: For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned. If you cannot look up at the crest of the deva-king Varuna's standard, then you should look up at the crest of the deva-king Isana's standard.

cbv16:6.1.12.verse: For when you look up at the crest of his standard, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.’

cbv16:6.1.13.verse: Bhikkhus, for those who look up at the crest of the standard of Sakka, lord of the devas;

cbv16:6.1.14.verse: or of Pajapati, the deva-king; or of Varuna, the deva-king;

cbv16:6.1.15.verse: or of Isana, the deva-king, whatever fear or trepidation or terror they may have may or may not be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.17.verse: Because Sakka, lord of the devas, is not devoid of lust, not devoid of hatred, not devoid of delusion; he can be timid, petrified, frightened, quick to flee.

cbv16:6.1.19.verse: If you have gone to a forest or to the foot of a tree or to an empty hut, and fear or trepidation or terror should arise in you, on that occasion you should recollect me thus:

cbv16:6.1.20.verse: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ For when you recollect me,

cbv16:6.1.21.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.22.verse: If you cannot recollect me, then you should recollect the Dhamma thus:

cbv16:6.1.23.verse: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ For when you recollect the Dhamma,

cbv16:6.1.24.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.25.verse: If you cannot recollect the Dhamma, then you should recollect the Sangha thus:

cbv16:6.1.26.verse: ‘The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practising the good way, practising the straight way, practising the true way, practising the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals: this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ For when you recollect the Sangha,

cbv16:6.1.27.verse: bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or terror you may have will be abandoned.

cbv16:6.1.29.verse: Because, bhikkhus, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is devoid of lust, devoid of hatred, devoid of delusion; he is brave, courageous, bold, ready to stand his place.”

cbv16:6.1.30.verse: This is what the Blessed One said.

cbv16:6.1.31.verse: Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:

cbv16:6.1.32.verse: “In a forest, at the foot of a tree,

cbv16:6.1.33.verse: Or in an empty hut, O bhikkhus,

cbv16:6.1.35.verse: No fear will then arise in you.

cbv16:6.1.36.verse: But if you cannot recall the Buddha,

cbv16:6.1.37.verse: Best in the world, the bull of men,

cbv16:6.1.38.verse: Then you should recall the Dhamma,

cbv16:6.1.40.verse: But if you cannot recall the Dhamma,

cbv16:6.1.42.verse: Then you should recall the Sangha,

cbv16:6.1.44.verse: For those who thus recall the Buddha,

cbv16:6.1.45.verse: The Dhamma, and the Sangha, bhikkhus,

cbv16:6.1.47.verse: will arise, Nor any grisly terror.

cbv17:0.2.verse: The Factor of Awakening Concerning the Elder Mahā Kassapa

cbv17:2.1.verse: ° The elder Mahā Kassapa, having heard that safeguard

cbv17:2.2.verse: from the Sage, at that moment became free from adversity.

cbv17:2.3.verse: It is about the strength of the factors of Awakening, we will recite that safeguard.

cbv17:5.1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place in Bamboo Wood.

cbv17:5.1.2.verse: Then at that time venerable Mahā Kassapa was dwelling at the Pepper Cave, and was afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

cbv17:5.1.3.verse: Then the Fortunate One, rising from seclusion in the evening time, approached venerable Mahā Kassapa, and after approaching he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down the Fortunate One said this to venerable Mahā Kassapa:

cbv17:5.1.4.verse: “Can you bear up, Kassapa? Can you carry on? Do painful feelings decrease and not increase? Is it known that they are decreasing and not increasing?”

cbv17:5.1.5.verse: “No, reverend Sir, I cannot bear up, nor can I carry on, painful feelings greatly increase for me and do not decrease, and it is known that they increase and do not decrease.”

cbv17:5.1.6.verse: “There are these seven factors of Awakening, Kassapa, that have been fully explained by me, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:6.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is mindfulness, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:6.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:7.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is investigation of (the nature of) things, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:7.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:8.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is energy, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:8.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:9.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is rapture, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:9.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:10.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is calm, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:10.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:11.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is concentration, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:11.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:12.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is equanimity, Kassapa, has been fully explained by me,

cbv17:12.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv17:13.1.1.verse: These are the seven factors of Awakening, Kassapa, which have been fully explained by me, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.”

cbv17:13.1.2.verse: “Surely, Fortunate One, (these are) the factors of Awakening!

cbv17:13.1.3.verse: Surely, Happy One, (these are) the factors of Awakening!”

cbv17:13.1.5.verse: and venerable Mahā Kassapa was uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was said by the Fortunate One,

cbv17:13.1.6.verse: and venerable Mahā Kassapa recovered from that affliction,

cbv17:13.1.7.verse: and by that venerable Mahā Kassapa’s affliction was brought to an end.

cbv17:5.1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

cbv17:5.1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali cave, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

cbv17:5.1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat, went to Venerable Mahākassapa, sat down on the seat spread out, and said to him:

cbv17:5.1.4.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Kassapa, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

cbv17:5.1.5.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

cbv17:5.1.6.verse: “Kassapa, I’ve rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

cbv17:13.1.1.verse: These are the seven awakening factors that I’ve rightly explained. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.”

cbv17:13.1.2.verse: “Indeed, Blessed One, these are awakening factors!

cbv17:13.1.3.verse: Indeed, Holy One, these are awakening factors!”

cbv17:13.1.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

cbv17:13.1.5.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Mahākassapa approved what the Buddha said.

cbv17:13.1.6.verse: And that’s how he recovered from that illness.

cbv18:0.1.verse: The Factor of Awakening Concerning the Elder Mahā Moggallāna

cbv18:2.1.verse: ° The elder Mahā Moggallāna, having heard that safeguard

cbv18:2.2.verse: from the Sage, at that moment became free from adversity.

cbv18:2.3.verse: It is about the strength of the factors of Awakening, we will recite that safeguard.

cbv18:5.1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place in Bamboo Wood.

cbv18:5.1.2.verse: Then at that time venerable Mahā Moggallāna was dwelling at the Vultures’ Peak mountain, and was afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

cbv18:5.1.3.verse: Then the Fortunate One, rising from seclusion in the evening time, approached venerable Mahā Moggallāna, and after approaching he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down the Fortunate One said this to venerable Mahā Moggallāna:

cbv18:5.1.4.verse: “Can you bear up, Moggallāna? Can you carry on? Do painful feelings decrease and not increase? Is it known that they are decreasing and not increasing?”

cbv18:5.1.5.verse: “No, reverend Sir, I cannot bear up, nor can I carry on, painful feelings greatly increase for me and do not decrease, and it is known that they increase and do not decrease.”

cbv18:5.1.6.verse: “There are these seven factors of Awakening, Moggallāna, that have been fully explained by me, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:6.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is mindfulness, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:6.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:7.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is investigation of (the nature of) things, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:7.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:8.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is energy, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:8.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:9.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is rapture, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:9.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:10.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is calm, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:10.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:11.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is concentration, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:11.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:12.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is equanimity, Moggallāna, has been fully explained by me,

cbv18:12.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv18:13.1.1.verse: These are the seven factors of Awakening, Moggallāna, which have been fully explained by me, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.”

cbv18:13.1.2.verse: “Surely, Fortunate One, (these are) the factors of Awakening!

cbv18:13.1.3.verse: Surely, Happy One, (these are) the factors of Awakening!”

cbv18:13.1.5.verse: and venerable Mahā Moggallāna was uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was said by the Fortunate One,

cbv18:13.1.6.verse: and venerable Mahā Moggallāna recovered from that affliction,

cbv18:13.1.7.verse: and by that venerable Mahā Moggallāna’s affliction was brought to an end.

cbv18:5.1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

cbv18:5.1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

cbv18:5.1.3.verse: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat, went to Venerable Moggallāna, sat down on the seat spread out, and said to him:

cbv18:5.1.4.verse: “I hope you’re keeping well, Moggallāna, I hope you’re all right. I hope your pain is fading, not growing; that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

cbv18:5.1.5.verse: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. My pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”

cbv18:5.1.6.verse: “Moggallāna, I’ve rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

cbv18:13.1.1.verse: These are the seven awakening factors that I’ve rightly explained. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.”

cbv18:13.1.2.verse: “Indeed, Blessed One, these are awakening factors!

cbv18:13.1.3.verse: Indeed, Holy One, these are awakening factors!”

cbv18:13.1.4.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

cbv18:13.1.5.verse: Satisfied, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approved what the Buddha said.

cbv18:13.1.6.verse: And that’s how he recovered from that illness.

cbv19:0.1.verse: The Factor of Awakening Concerning the Elder Mahā Cunda

cbv19:2.1.verse: ° The Fortunate One, lord of the world, having heard this (safeguard)

cbv19:2.2.verse: from the elder Cunda, at that moment became free from adversity.

cbv19:2.3.verse: It is about the strength of the factors of Awakening, we will recite that safeguard.

cbv19:5.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha

cbv19:5.2.verse: at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place in Bamboo Wood.

cbv19:6.1.1.verse: Then at that time the Fortunate One was afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

cbv19:6.1.2.verse: Then venerable Mahā Cunda, rising from seclusion in the evening time, approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, he sat down on one side. While he was sitting on one side the Fortunate One said this to venerable Mahā Cunda:

cbv19:6.1.3.verse: “May the factors of Awakening occur to you, Cunda.”

cbv19:6.1.4.verse: “There are these seven factors of Awakening, reverend Sir, that have been fully explained by the Fortunate One, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:7.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is mindfulness, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:7.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:8.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is investigation of (the nature of) things, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:8.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:9.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is energy, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:9.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:10.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is rapture, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:10.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:11.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is calm, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:11.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:12.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is concentration, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:12.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:13.1.verse: The factor of Complete Awakening that is equanimity, reverend Sir, has been fully explained by the Fortunate One,

cbv19:13.2.verse: when developed and made much of it leads to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv19:14.1.1.verse: These are the seven factors of Awakening, reverend Sir, which have been fully explained by the Fortunate One, when developed and made much of they lead to deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.”

cbv19:14.1.2.verse: “Surely, Cunda, (these are) the factors of Awakening!

cbv19:14.1.3.verse: Surely, Cunda, (these are) the factors of Awakening!”

cbv19:14.1.5.verse: and the Teacher was in agreement,

cbv19:14.1.6.verse: and the Fortunate One recovered from that affliction,

cbv19:14.1.7.verse: and by that the Fortunate One’s affliction was brought to an end.

cbv19:6.1.1.verse: Now at that time he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

cbv19:6.1.2.verse: Then Venerable Mahācunda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

cbv19:6.1.3.verse: “Cunda, express your understanding of the awakening factors.”

cbv19:6.1.4.verse: “Sir, the Buddha has rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

cbv19:14.1.1.verse: These are the seven awakening factors that the Buddha has rightly explained. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.”

cbv19:14.1.3.verse: Indeed, Cunda, these are awakening factors!”

cbv19:14.1.6.verse: And that’s how the Buddha recovered from that illness.

cbv20:2.1.verse: ° The elder Girimānanda, having heard that (safeguard)

cbv20:2.2.verse: from the elder Ānanda, at that moment became free from adversity.

cbv20:2.3.verse: It is about the ten perceptions, we will recite that safeguard.

cbv20:5.1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv20:5.1.2.verse: Then at that time venerable Girimānanda was afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

cbv20:5.1.3.verse: Then venerable Ānanda approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, he sat down on one side. While sitting on one side venerable Ānanda said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv20:5.1.4.verse: “Reverend Sir, venerable Girimānanda is afflicted, suffering, and very sick.

cbv20:5.1.5.verse: Please, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One approach venerable Girimānanda, taking pity on him.”

cbv20:5.1.6.verse: “If you, Ānanda, having approached the monk Girimānanda, were to recite the ten perceptions, then it is possible that having heard the ten perceptions, the monk Girimānanda’s affliction would immediately abate.

cbv20:5.1.8.verse: The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of giving up, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of impermanence in all processes, mindfulness while breathing.

cbv20:5.1.9.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence?

cbv20:5.1.10.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

cbv20:5.1.11.verse: form is impermanent, feelings are impermanent, perceptions are impermanent, (mental) processes are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.

cbv20:5.1.12.verse: Thus in regard to these five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment he dwells contemplating impermanence.

cbv20:5.1.13.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of impermanence.

cbv20:5.1.14.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self?

cbv20:5.1.15.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

cbv20:5.1.16.verse: the eye is not self - forms are not self, the ear is not self - sounds are not self, the nose is not self - smells are not self, the tongue is not self - tastes are not self, the body is not self - tangibles are not self, the mind is not self - thoughts are not self.

cbv20:5.1.17.verse: Thus in regard to these six internal and external sense spheres he dwells contemplating non-self.

cbv20:5.1.18.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-self.

cbv20:5.1.19.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of the unattractive?

cbv20:5.1.20.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk (in regard to) this body - from the sole of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head down, bounded by the skin, and filled with manifold impurities - reflects (thus):

cbv20:5.1.21.verse: There are in this body: hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, excrement, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spit, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.

cbv20:5.1.22.verse: Thus in regard to this body he dwells contemplating what is unattractive.

cbv20:5.1.23.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of the unattractive.

cbv20:5.1.24.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger?

cbv20:5.1.25.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

cbv20:5.1.26.verse: This body has many sufferings, many dangers, thus, in connection with this body, various afflictions arise, like this:

cbv20:5.1.27.verse: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease (i.e diseases affecting the sense spheres), head-disease, ear-disease, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, pyrexia, fever, stomach-ache, fainting, diarrhoea, gripes, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scab, chickenpox, scabies, haemorrhage, diabetes, piles, cancer, ulcers, afflictions arising from excess bile, afflictions arising from excess phlegm, afflictions arising from excess wind, afflictions arising from a conflict of humours, afflictions born of a change of season, afflictions born of not being careful, afflictions from being attacked, afflictions born as a result of (previous unwholesome) actions, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, stool, urine.

cbv20:5.1.28.verse: Thus, in regard to this body, he dwells contemplating danger.

cbv20:5.1.29.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.

cbv20:5.1.30.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of giving up?

cbv20:5.1.31.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk does not consent to thoughts of sense desire that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to thoughts of ill-will that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to thoughts of violence that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent. He does not consent to any bad, unwholesome, thoughts that have arisen, (these) he gives up, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent.

cbv20:5.1.32.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of giving up.

cbv20:5.1.33.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of dispassion?

cbv20:5.1.34.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

cbv20:5.1.35.verse: This is peaceful, this is excellent, that is to say: the calming of all processes, the letting go of all bases for cleaving, the end of craving, dispassion, Nibbāna.

cbv20:5.1.36.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of dispassion.

cbv20:5.1.37.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation?

cbv20:5.1.38.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, considers thus:

cbv20:5.1.39.verse: This is peaceful, this is excellent, that is to say: the calming of all processes, the letting go of all bases for cleaving, the end of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.

cbv20:5.1.40.verse: This, Ānanda, is called the perception of cessation.

cbv20:5.1.41.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world?

cbv20:5.1.42.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk in regard to whatever in the world are selfish means and attachments, or mental determinations, settled beliefs, and tendencies, giving these up, not being attached, he abstains (from them).

cbv20:5.1.43.verse: This, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world.

cbv20:5.1.44.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence in all processes?

cbv20:5.1.45.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk in regard to all processes is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.

cbv20:5.1.46.verse: This, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence in all processes.

cbv20:5.1.47.verse: Now what, Ānanda, is mindfulness while breathing?

cbv20:5.1.48.verse: Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down. After folding his legs crosswise, setting his body straight, and establishing mindfulness at the front,

cbv20:5.1.49.verse: mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.

cbv20:5.1.50.verse: While breathing in long, he knows “I am breathing in long”, while breathing out long, he knows “I am breathing out long”,

cbv20:5.1.51.verse: while breathing in short, he knows “I am breathing in short”, while breathing out short, he knows “I am breathing out short”,

cbv20:5.1.52.verse: he trains like this: experiencing the whole body I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the whole body I will breathe out,

cbv20:5.1.53.verse: he trains like this: making the bodily process calm I will breathe in, he trains like this: making the bodily process calm I will breathe out.

cbv20:5.1.54.verse: He trains like this: experiencing joy I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing happiness I will breathe out,

cbv20:5.1.55.verse: he trains like this: experiencing pleasure I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing pleasure I will breathe out,

cbv20:5.1.56.verse: he trains like this: experiencing the mental process I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the mental process I will breathe out,

cbv20:5.1.57.verse: he trains like this: making the mental process calm I will breathe in, he trains like this: making the mental process calm I will breathe out.

cbv20:5.1.58.verse: He trains like this: experiencing the mind I will breathe in, he trains like this: experiencing the mind I will breathe out,

cbv20:6.1.verse: he trains like this: gladdening the mind I will breathe in,

cbv20:6.2.verse: he trains like this: gladdening the mind I will breathe out,

cbv20:7.1.verse: he trains like this: concentrating the mind I will breathe in,

cbv20:7.2.verse: he trains like this: concentrating the mind I will breathe out,

cbv20:8.1.verse: he trains like this: freeing the mind I will breathe in,

cbv20:8.2.verse: he trains like this: freeing the mind I will breathe out.

cbv20:9.1.verse: he trains like this: contemplating impermanence I will breathe in,

cbv20:9.2.verse: he trains like this: contemplating impermanence I will breathe out,

cbv20:10.1.verse: he trains like this: contemplating dispassion I will breathe in,

cbv20:10.2.verse: he trains like this: contemplating dispassion I will breathe out,

cbv20:11.1.verse: he trains like this: contemplating cessation I will breathe in,

cbv20:11.2.verse: he trains like this: contemplating cessation I will breathe out,

cbv20:12.1.1.verse: he trains like this: contemplating letting go I will breathe in, he trains like this: contemplating letting go I will breathe out.

cbv20:12.1.2.verse: This, Ānanda, is mindfulness while breathing.

cbv20:12.1.3.verse: If you, Ānanda, having approached the monk Girimānanda, were to recite these ten percpetions, then it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, the monk Girimānanda’s affliction would immediately abate.”

cbv20:12.1.4.verse: Then venerable Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions from the Fortunate One, approached venerable Girimānanda, and after approaching he recited these ten perceptions to venerable Girimānanda.

cbv20:12.1.5.verse: Then, having heard these ten perceptions, venerable Girimānanda’s affliction immediately abated,

cbv20:12.1.6.verse: and venerable Girimānanda recovered from that affliction, and by that venerable Girimānanda’s affliction was brought to an end.

cbv20:5.1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

cbv20:5.1.2.verse: Now at that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

cbv20:5.1.3.verse: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

cbv20:5.1.4.verse: “Sir, Venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, gravely ill.

cbv20:5.1.5.verse: Sir, please go to Venerable Girimānanda out of sympathy.”

cbv20:5.1.6.verse: “Ānanda, if you were to recite to the mendicant Girimānanda these ten perceptions, it’s possible that after hearing them his illness will die down on the spot.

cbv20:5.1.8.verse: The perceptions of impermanence, not-self, ugliness, drawbacks, giving up, fading away, cessation, dissatisfaction with the whole world, impermanence of all conditions, and mindfulness of breathing.

cbv20:5.1.9.verse: And what is the perception of impermanence?

cbv20:5.1.10.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

cbv20:5.1.11.verse: ‘Form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are impermanent.’

cbv20:5.1.12.verse: And so they meditate observing impermanence in the five grasping aggregates.

cbv20:5.1.13.verse: This is called the perception of impermanence.

cbv20:5.1.14.verse: And what is the perception of not-self?

cbv20:5.1.15.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

cbv20:5.1.16.verse: ‘The eye and sights, ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and tastes, body and touches, and mind and ideas are not-self.’

cbv20:5.1.17.verse: And so they meditate observing not-self in the six interior and exterior sense fields.

cbv20:5.1.18.verse: This is called the perception of not-self.

cbv20:5.1.19.verse: And what is the perception of ugliness?

cbv20:5.1.20.verse: It’s when a mendicant examines their own body up from the soles of the feet and down from the tips of the hairs, wrapped in skin and full of many kinds of filth.

cbv20:5.1.21.verse: ‘In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’

cbv20:5.1.22.verse: And so they meditate observing ugliness in this body.

cbv20:5.1.23.verse: This is called the perception of ugliness.

cbv20:5.1.24.verse: And what is the perception of drawbacks?

cbv20:5.1.25.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

cbv20:5.1.26.verse: ‘This body has much suffering and many drawbacks. For this body is beset with many kinds of affliction, such as the following.

cbv20:5.1.27.verse: Diseases of the eye, inner ear, nose, tongue, body, head, outer ear, mouth, teeth, and lips. Cough, asthma, catarrh, inflammation, fever, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, gastric pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, herpes, itch, scabs, smallpox, scabies, hemorrhage, diabetes, piles, pimples, and ulcers. Afflictions stemming from disorders of bile, phlegm, wind, or their conjunction. Afflictions caused by change in weather, by not taking care of yourself, by exertion, or as the result of past deeds. Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.’

cbv20:5.1.28.verse: And so they meditate observing drawbacks in this body.

cbv20:5.1.29.verse: This is called the perception of drawbacks.

cbv20:5.1.30.verse: And what is the perception of giving up?

cbv20:5.1.31.verse: It’s when a mendicant doesn’t tolerate a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought that has arisen, and they don’t tolerate any bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them.

cbv20:5.1.32.verse: This is called the perception of giving up.

cbv20:5.1.33.verse: And what is the perception of fading away?

cbv20:5.1.34.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

cbv20:5.1.35.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, extinguishment.’

cbv20:5.1.36.verse: This is called the perception of fading away.

cbv20:5.1.37.verse: And what is the perception of cessation?

cbv20:5.1.38.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

cbv20:5.1.39.verse: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, cessation, extinguishment.’

cbv20:5.1.40.verse: This is called the perception of cessation.

cbv20:5.1.41.verse: And what is the perception of dissatisfaction with the whole world?

cbv20:5.1.42.verse: It’s when a mendicant lives giving up and not grasping on to the attraction and grasping to the world, the mental fixation, insistence, and underlying tendencies.

cbv20:5.1.43.verse: This is called the perception of dissatisfaction with the whole world.

cbv20:5.1.44.verse: And what is the perception of the impermanence of all conditions?

cbv20:5.1.45.verse: It’s when a mendicant is horrified, repelled, and disgusted with all conditions.

cbv20:5.1.46.verse: This is called the perception of the impermanence of all conditions.

cbv20:5.1.47.verse: And what is mindfulness of breathing?

cbv20:5.1.48.verse: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.

cbv20:5.1.49.verse: Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.

cbv20:5.1.50.verse: Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’

cbv20:5.1.51.verse: Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’

cbv20:5.1.52.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’

cbv20:5.1.53.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’

cbv20:5.1.54.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing rapture.’

cbv20:5.1.55.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing bliss.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing bliss.’

cbv20:5.1.56.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mental process.’

cbv20:5.1.57.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the mental process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the mental process.’

cbv20:5.1.58.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the mind.’

cbv20:12.1.1.verse: They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in observing letting go.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out observing letting go.’

cbv20:12.1.2.verse: This is called mindfulness of breathing.

cbv20:12.1.3.verse: If you were to recite to the mendicant Girimānanda these ten perceptions, it’s possible that after hearing them his illness will die down on the spot.”

cbv20:12.1.4.verse: Then Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions from the Buddha himself, went to Girimānanda and recited them.

cbv20:12.1.5.verse: Then after Girimānanda heard these ten perceptions his illness died down on the spot.

cbv20:12.1.6.verse: And that’s how he recovered from that illness.

cbv22:0.2.verse: The Discourse that Set the Dhamma Wheel Rolling

cbv22:1.1.verse: Reverence to him, the Fortunate One, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha

cbv22:3.1.1.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

cbv22:3.1.2.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the group-of-five monks, saying:

cbv22:4.1.1.verse: “There are these two extremes, monks, that one who has gone forth ought not to associate with,

cbv22:4.1.3.verse: which is this: devotion to the pleasure and happiness in sense pleasures, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected with the goal; and this: devotion to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and not connected with the goal.

cbv22:4.1.4.verse: Not having approached either of these two extremes, monks, the middle practice was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv22:4.1.5.verse: Now what is this middle practice, monks, that was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna?

cbv22:4.1.6.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

cbv22:4.1.7.verse: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right endeavour, right mindfulness, right concentration.

cbv22:4.1.8.verse: This is the middle practice, monks, that was awakened to by the Realised One, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and which leads to peace, deep knowledge, Complete Awakening, and Nibbāna.

cbv22:6.1.1.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering:

cbv22:6.1.2.verse: birth is suffering, also old age is suffering, also sickness is suffering, also death is suffering, being joined to what is not dear is suffering, being separated from what is dear is suffering, also not to obtain what one longs for is suffering, in brief, the five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment are suffering.

cbv22:6.1.3.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the arising of suffering:

cbv22:6.1.4.verse: it is that craving which leads to continuation in existence, which is connected with enjoyment and passion, greatly enjoying this and that, as follows:

cbv22:6.1.5.verse: craving for sense pleasures, craving for continuation, craving for discontinuation.

cbv22:6.1.6.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering:

cbv22:6.1.7.verse: it is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that craving - liberation, letting go, release, and non-adherence.

cbv22:6.1.8.verse: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering:

cbv22:6.1.9.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

cbv22:9.1.1.verse: “This is the noble truth of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:10.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of suffering” refers (i.e. suffering itself) ought to be fully known -

cbv22:10.2.verse: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things

cbv22:10.3.verse: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,

cbv22:11.1.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of suffering” refers has been fully known - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:11.1.2.verse: “This is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:12.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” refers (i.e. craving) ought to be given up -

cbv22:12.2.verse: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things

cbv22:12.3.verse: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,

cbv22:13.1.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” refers has been given up, to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:13.1.2.verse: “This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:14.1.verse: Now that to which this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” refers (i.e. Nibbāna) ought to be experienced -

cbv22:14.2.verse: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things

cbv22:14.3.verse: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,

cbv22:15.1.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” refers has been experienced - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:15.1.2.verse: “This is the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering”- to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:16.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering” refers (i.e. the practice itself) -

cbv22:16.3.verse: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things

cbv22:16.4.verse: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,

cbv22:17.1.1.verse: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering” refers - has been developed - to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose, understanding arose, light arose.

cbv22:19.1.1.verse: For as long as to me, monks, in regard to these four noble truths - turned like this, in three ways, twelvefold - knowledge and insight as it really is was not quite clear, for that long, monks, I did not declare to the world with its gods, Māra, and Brahma, to this generation, with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men, that I was fully awakened with unsurpassed complete awakening.

cbv22:19.1.2.verse: But when to me, monks, in regard to these four noble truths - turned like this, in three ways, twelvefold - knowledge and insight as it really is was quite clear then, monks, I did declare to the world with its gods, Māra, and Brahma, to this generation, with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men, that I was fully awakened with unsurpassed complete awakening.

cbv22:19.1.3.verse: To me knowledge and seeing arose:

cbv22:19.1.4.verse: “Sure is my freedom of mind this is my last birth now there is no continuation of existence.”

cbv22:21.1.2.verse: and the group-of-five monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was said by the Fortunate One.

cbv22:21.1.3.verse: Moreover, as this sermon was being given, to venerable Koṇḍañña the dust-free, stainless, Vision-of-the-Dhamma arose:

cbv22:21.1.4.verse: Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing.

cbv22:67.1.2.verse: and this ten thousand world-element moved, wavered, and shook, and great and measureless light became manifest in the world, transcending the psychic power of the gods.
