cbv22:67.1.5.verse: Thus to the venerable Koṇḍañña came the name Aññā Koṇḍañña (Koṇḍañña, he-who-knows).

cbv22:3.1.1.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

cbv22:3.1.2.verse: There the Buddha addressed the group of five mendicants:

cbv22:4.1.1.verse: “Mendicants, these two extremes should not be cultivated by one gone forth.

cbv22:4.1.3.verse: Indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And indulgence in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless.

cbv22:4.1.4.verse: Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

cbv22:4.1.5.verse: And what is that middle way of practice?

cbv22:4.1.6.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

cbv22:4.1.7.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

cbv22:4.1.8.verse: This is that middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment.

cbv22:6.1.1.verse: Now this is the noble truth of suffering.

cbv22:6.1.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

cbv22:6.1.3.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

cbv22:6.1.4.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

cbv22:6.1.5.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

cbv22:6.1.6.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

cbv22:6.1.7.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

cbv22:6.1.8.verse: Now this is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

cbv22:6.1.9.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

cbv22:9.1.1.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.

cbv22:11.1.1.verse: ‘This noble truth of suffering has been completely understood.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:11.1.2.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:13.1.1.verse: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been given up.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:13.1.2.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:15.1.1.verse: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:15.1.2.verse: ‘This is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ Such was the vision that arose in me …

cbv22:17.1.1.verse: ‘This noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering has been developed.’ Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.

cbv22:19.1.1.verse: As long as my true knowledge and vision about these four noble truths was not fully purified in these three rounds and twelve aspects, I didn’t announce my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

cbv22:19.1.2.verse: But when my true knowledge and vision about these four noble truths was fully purified in these three rounds and twelve aspects, I announced my supreme perfect awakening in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans.

cbv22:19.1.3.verse: Knowledge and vision arose in me:

cbv22:19.1.4.verse: ‘My freedom is unshakable; this is my last rebirth; now there’ll be no more future lives.’”

cbv22:21.1.1.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

cbv22:21.1.2.verse: Satisfied, the group of five mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

cbv22:21.1.3.verse: And while this discourse was being spoken, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in Venerable Koṇḍañña:

cbv22:21.1.4.verse: “Everything that is liable to arise is liable to cease.”

cbv22:23.1.1.verse: And when the Buddha rolled forth the Wheel of Dhamma, the earth gods raised the cry:

cbv22:23.1.2.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Buddha has rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.”

cbv22:24.1.1.verse: Hearing the cry of the earth gods, the gods of the four great kings …

cbv22:67.1.1.verse: And so at that moment, that second, that hour, the cry soared up to the realm of divinity.

cbv22:67.1.2.verse: And this ten-thousandfold galaxy shook and rocked and trembled. And an immeasurable, magnificent light appeared in the world, surpassing the glory of the gods.

cbv22:67.1.3.verse: Then the Buddha expressed this heartfelt sentiment:

cbv22:67.1.4.verse: “Koṇḍañña has really understood! Koṇḍañña has really understood!”

cbv22:67.1.5.verse: And that’s how Venerable Koṇḍañña came to be known as “Koṇḍañña Who Understood”.

cbv23:0.1.verse: The Discourse on the Great Convention

cbv23:1.1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling amongst the Sakyans in the Great Wood near Kapilavatthu with a great Saṅgha of monks consisting of five hundred monks, all of them Worthy Ones,

cbv23:1.1.3.verse: and almost all of the gods from the ten world-elements had assembled to see the Fortunate One and the Saṅgha of monks.

cbv23:1.1.4.verse: Then this occurred to four gods from among the hosts in the Pure Abodes:

cbv23:1.1.5.verse: “The Fortunate One is dwelling amongst the Sakyans in the Great Wood near Kapilavatthu with a great Saṅgha of moṅks consisting of five hundred monks, all of them Worthy Ones,

cbv23:1.1.6.verse: and almost all of the gods from the ten world elements have assembled to see the Fortunate One and the Saṅgha of monks.

cbv23:1.1.7.verse: Well now, we too could approach the Fortunate One, and after approaching the Fortunate One we could recite a verse each in his presence.”

cbv23:1.1.8.verse: Then those gods, just as a strong man might stretch out a bent arm, or bend in an outstretched arm, in the same way disappeared from among the gods of the Pure Abodes and appeared in front of the Fortunate One.

cbv23:1.1.9.verse: Then those gods after worshipping the Fortunate One, stood on one side.

cbv23:1.1.10.verse: While standing on one side one of the gods recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

cbv23:1.1.11.verse: “There is a great convention in the wood,

cbv23:1.1.12.verse: and a host of gods have come,

cbv23:1.1.13.verse: we have come to this Dhamma convention

cbv23:1.1.14.verse: to see the Saṅgha, who are undefeated.”

cbv23:1.1.15.verse: Then another god recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

cbv23:1.1.16.verse: “In this place the monks are concentrated,

cbv23:1.1.17.verse: they have straightened out their minds by themselves,

cbv23:1.1.18.verse: like a charioteer who has taken the reins,

cbv23:1.1.19.verse: the wise protect their sense faculties.”

cbv23:1.1.20.verse: Then another god recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

cbv23:1.1.21.verse: “Having cut off the hindrance and obstacle,

cbv23:1.1.22.verse: and dug up the locking post, they are unmoved,

cbv23:1.1.24.verse: young nāgas, well-tamed by the Visionary.”

cbv23:1.1.25.verse: Then another god recited this verse in the presence of the Fortunate One:

cbv23:1.1.26.verse: “Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge

cbv23:1.1.27.verse: will not go to the lower worlds.

cbv23:1.1.28.verse: After giving up the human body

cbv23:1.1.29.verse: they will fill up the ranks of the gods.”

cbv23:1.1.31.verse: Then the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

cbv23:1.1.32.verse: “Monks, almost all of the gods from the ten world-elements have assembled to see the Realised One and the Saṅgha of monks.

cbv23:1.1.33.verse: Monks, those who in the past were Worthy Ones, Perfect Sambuddhas, for those Fortunate Ones also at least as many gods have assembled as for me at the present time.

cbv23:1.1.34.verse: Monks, those who in the future will be Worthy Ones, Perfect Sambuddhas, for those Fortunate Ones also at least as many gods will assemble as for me at the present time.

cbv23:1.1.35.verse: Monks, I will declare the names of the hosts of gods,

cbv23:1.1.36.verse: monks, I will proclaim the names of the hosts of gods,

cbv23:1.1.37.verse: monks, I will reveal the names of the hosts of gods.

cbv23:1.1.38.verse: Listen to it, apply your minds well, and I will speak.”

cbv23:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, in the Great Wood near Kapilavatthu, together with a large Saṅgha of five hundred mendicants, all of whom were perfected ones.

cbv23:1.1.3.verse: And most of the deities from ten solar systems had gathered to see the Buddha and the Saṅgha of mendicants.

cbv23:1.1.4.verse: Then four deities of the pure abodes, aware of what was happening, thought:

cbv23:1.1.7.verse: “Why don’t we go to the Buddha and each recite a verse in his presence?”

cbv25:1.1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling amongst the Magadhans on the Southern Hill near the brahmin village Ekanālā.

cbv25:1.1.3.verse: Then at that time the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja had about five hundred ploughs yoked up during the sowing season.

cbv25:1.1.4.verse: Then the Fortunate One, having dressed in the morning time, after picking up his bowl and robe, approached the place where the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja was working.

cbv25:1.1.5.verse: Then at that time the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja’s food distribution was proceeding.

cbv25:1.1.6.verse: Then the Fortunate One approached the food distribution, and after approaching he stood on one side.

cbv25:1.1.7.verse: The brahmin Kasībhāradvāja saw the Fortunate One standing for alms,

cbv25:1.1.8.verse: and after seeing him he said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv25:1.1.9.verse: “Ascetic, I plough and I sow, and after ploughing and sowing I eat.

cbv25:1.1.10.verse: You also, ascetic, should plough and sow, and after ploughing and sowing you can eat.”

cbv25:1.1.11.verse: “Brahmin, I also plough and sow, and after ploughing and sowing I eat.”

cbv25:1.1.12.verse: “But we do not see the reverend Gotama’s yoke or plough or ploughshare or goad or oxen, but still the reverend Gotama said this:

cbv25:1.1.13.verse: ‘Brahmin, I also plough and sow, and after ploughing and sowing I eat.’ ”

cbv25:1.1.14.verse: Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja recited a verse to the Fortunate One:

cbv25:1.1.15.verse: “You claim that you are a ploughman,

cbv25:1.1.16.verse: but we do not see your ploughing.

cbv25:1.1.17.verse: Please tell us about ploughing when asked

cbv25:1.1.18.verse: so that we may know your ploughing.”

cbv25:3.1.8.verse: Another great sage, who is fully adept,

cbv25:3.1.9.verse: pollutant-free, at peace regarding worry (about wrong-doing),

cbv25:3.1.10.verse: attend to with food and drink,

cbv25:3.1.11.verse: for that is the field for those who look for merit.”

cbv25:4.1.verse: “Then to whom, reverend Gotama, should I give this milk-rice?”

cbv25:5.1.verse: “I certainly do not see, brahmin, in the world with its gods, Māra, and Brahma,

cbv25:5.2.verse: in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and men,

cbv25:5.3.verse: anyone who, having eaten this milk-rice, could properly digest it,

cbv25:5.4.verse: except a Realised One or a Realised One’s disciple.

cbv25:6.1.verse: Therefore, brahmin, cast away that milk-rice where there is but little grass,

cbv25:6.2.verse: or drop it into water which has no breathing creatures.”

cbv25:7.1.verse: Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja dropped that milk-rice into water which had no breathing creatures.

cbv25:8.1.verse: Then that milk-rice being thrown into water

cbv25:8.2.verse: did hiss and sizzle and steam and smoke,

cbv25:9.1.verse: just as a ploughshare heated for a day when thrown into water

cbv25:9.2.verse: hisses and sizzles and steams and smokes,

cbv25:10.1.verse: so that milk-rice being thrown into water

cbv25:10.2.verse: did hiss and sizzle and steam and smoke.

cbv25:11.1.verse: Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, anxious, and horrified,

cbv25:11.3.verse: and after approaching he fell down placing his head at the Fortunate One’s feet,

cbv25:11.4.verse: and said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv25:13.1.verse: Just as, reverend Gotama, one might set upright what has been overturned,

cbv25:13.2.verse: or open up what has been closed, or show a path to one who is lost,

cbv25:13.3.verse: or bear an oil lamp in the darkness so that one who has eyes can see forms,

cbv25:13.4.verse: just so has the Dhamma been made clear by reverend Gotama in more than one way.

cbv25:14.1.verse: I go to the reverend Gotama for refuge,

cbv25:14.2.verse: and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.

cbv25:15.1.verse: May I receive the going forth in the presence of reverend Gotama,

cbv25:15.2.verse: may I receive the full ordination.”

cbv25:16.2.verse: the going forth in the presence of the Fortunate One, received full ordination.

cbv25:17.1.verse: Then not long after ordination, venerable Bhāradvāja,

cbv25:17.2.verse: while dwelling solitary, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute,

cbv25:17.3.verse: after no long time (attained) that good for which young gentlemen

cbv25:17.4.verse: rightly go forth from the house to the houseless life,

cbv25:17.5.verse: that unsurpassed conclusion to the spiritual life,

cbv25:17.6.verse: and dwelt having known, experienced, and attained it himself in this very life.

cbv25:18.3.verse: done is what ought to be done

cbv25:18.4.verse: there is no more of this mundane state - this he knew.

cbv25:19.1.verse: And venerable Bhāradvāja became another of the Worthy Ones.

cbv25:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Magadhans in the Southern Hills near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa.

cbv25:1.1.3.verse: Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Farmer had harnessed around five hundred plows, it being the season for sowing.

cbv25:1.1.4.verse: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to where Bhāradvāja the Farmer was working.

cbv25:1.1.5.verse: Now at that time Bhāradvāja the Farmer was distributing food.

cbv25:1.1.6.verse: Then the Buddha went to where the distribution was taking place and stood to one side.

cbv25:1.1.7.verse: Bhāradvāja the Farmer saw him standing for alms

cbv25:1.1.9.verse: “I plough and sow, ascetic, and then I eat.

cbv25:1.1.10.verse: You too should plough and sow, then you may eat.”

cbv25:1.1.11.verse: “I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat.”

cbv25:1.1.12.verse: “I don’t see the worthy Gotama with a yoke or plow or plowshare or goad or oxen, yet he says:

cbv25:1.1.13.verse: ‘I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat.’”

cbv25:1.1.14.verse: Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer addressed the Buddha in verse:

cbv25:1.1.16.verse: but I don’t see you farming.

cbv25:1.1.17.verse: Tell me how you’re a farmer when asked:

cbv25:1.1.18.verse: how am I to recognize your farming?”

cbv25:1.1.19.verse: “Faith is my seed, fervor my rain,

cbv25:1.1.20.verse: and wisdom is my yoke and plough.

cbv25:1.1.21.verse: Conscience is my draft-pole, mind my strap,

cbv25:1.1.24.verse: I restrict my intake of food.

cbv25:1.1.25.verse: I use truth as my scythe,

cbv25:1.1.28.verse: transporting me to sanctuary from the yoke.

cbv25:1.1.30.verse: to where there is no sorrow.

cbv25:1.1.31.verse: That’s how to do the farming

cbv25:1.1.32.verse: that has freedom from death as its fruit.

cbv25:3.1.2.verse: The worthy one is a farmer.

cbv25:3.1.3.verse: For the worthy Gotama does the farming that has freedom from death as its fruit.”

cbv25:3.1.4.verse: “Food enchanted by a verse isn’t fit for me to eat.

cbv25:3.1.5.verse: That’s not the principle of those who see, brahmin.

cbv25:3.1.6.verse: The Buddhas cast aside things enchanted with verses.

cbv25:3.1.7.verse: Since there is such a principle, brahmin, that’s how they live.

cbv25:3.1.8.verse: Serve with other food and drink

cbv25:3.1.9.verse: the consummate one, the great seer,

cbv25:3.1.10.verse: with defilements ended and remorse stilled.

cbv25:3.1.11.verse: For he is the field for the seeker of merit.”

cbv25:1.1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Dakkhiṇāgiri near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa.

cbv25:1.1.3.verse: Now on that occasion the brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja the Ploughman, had five hundred ploughs fastened to their yokes at the time of sowing.

cbv25:1.1.4.verse: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed and, taking bowl and robe, went to the place where the brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja was at work.

cbv25:1.1.5.verse: Now on that occasion the brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja’s food distribution was taking place.

cbv25:1.1.6.verse: Then the Blessed One approached the place of the food distribution  and stood to one side.

cbv25:1.1.7.verse: The brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms

cbv25:1.1.9.verse: “Recluse, I plough and sow, and when I have ploughed and sown I eat.

cbv25:1.1.10.verse: You too, ascetic, ought to plough and sow; then, when you have ploughed and sown, you will eat. ”

cbv25:1.1.11.verse: “I too, brahmin, plough and sow, and when I have ploughed and sown I eat. ”

cbv25:1.1.12.verse: “But we do not see Master Gotama’s yoke or plough or ploughshare or goad or oxen; yet Master Gotama says, ‘I too, brahmin, plough and sow, and when I have ploughed and sown I eat. ’”

cbv25:1.1.14.verse: Then the brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One in verse:

cbv25:1.1.15.verse: “You claim to be a man who works the plough,

cbv25:1.1.16.verse: But I do not see your ploughing.

cbv25:1.1.17.verse: If you’re a ploughman, answer me:

cbv25:1.1.18.verse: How should we understand your ploughing?”

cbv25:1.1.19.verse: [The Blessed One: ]  “Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,

cbv25:1.1.21.verse: Shame is the pole, mind the yoke-tie,

cbv25:1.1.24.verse: Controlled in my appetite for food,

cbv25:1.1.25.verse: I use truth as my weeding-hook,

cbv25:1.1.28.verse: Carrying me to security from bondage.

cbv25:1.1.30.verse: To where, having gone, one does not sorrow .

cbv25:1.1.31.verse: “In such a way this ploughing is done

cbv25:1.1.32.verse: Which has the Deathless as its fruit.

cbv25:1.1.33.verse: Having finished this work of ploughing,

cbv25:1.1.34.verse: One is released from all suffering. ”

cbv25:3.1.3.verse: since Master Gotama does ploughing that has even the Deathless as its fruit. ”

cbv25:3.1.4.verse: “Food over which verses have been sung

cbv25:3.1.11.verse: For he is the field for one seeking merit. ”

cbv27:1.1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.

cbv27:1.1.3.verse: Then the Fortunate One, having dressed in the morning time, after picking up his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.

cbv27:1.1.4.verse: Then at that time in the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja’s residence the (sacrificial) fire was burning, and the offering had been taken up.

cbv27:1.1.5.verse: Then, as the Fortunate One was going from house to house for alms in Sāvatthī, he approached the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja’s residence.

cbv27:1.1.6.verse: The brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja saw the Fortunate One coming from afar,

cbv27:1.1.7.verse: and having seen him, he said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv27:1.1.11.verse: After this was said, the Fortunate One said this to the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja:

cbv27:1.1.12.verse: “But do you know, brahmin, what an outcaste is, or what things make one an outcaste?”

cbv27:1.1.13.verse: “I certainly do not know, reverend Gotama, what an outcaste is, or what things make one an outcaste.

cbv27:1.1.14.verse: It would be good for me if the reverend Gotama would preach the Dhamma so that I may know what an outcaste is, and what things make one an outcaste.”

cbv27:1.1.15.verse: “Then listen, brahmin, apply your mind well, and I will speak.”

cbv27:1.1.16.verse: “Yes, reverend,” the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja replied to the Fortunate One,

cbv27:1.1.17.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

cbv27:1.1.18.verse: “That man who is angry, who has enmity,

cbv28:0.1.verse: The Discourse giving the Analysis of the Truths

cbv28:1.1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

cbv28:1.1.3.verse: There it was that the Fortunate One addressed the monks, saying:

cbv28:1.1.5.verse: “Reverend Sir!” those monks replied to the Fortunate One,

cbv28:1.1.6.verse: and the Fortunate One said this:

cbv28:1.1.7.verse: “The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.8.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the four noble truths.

cbv28:1.1.10.verse: ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the arising of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. ° The explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:1.1.11.verse: “The Realised One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.12.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of these four noble truths.

cbv28:1.1.13.verse: Associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks,

cbv28:1.1.14.verse: keep company with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks,

cbv28:1.1.15.verse: they are wise monks who assist those living the spiritual life.

cbv28:1.1.16.verse: Sāriputta is just like one who gives birth, monks,

cbv28:1.1.17.verse: Moggallāna is just like a wet nurse to the one new-born, monks;

cbv28:1.1.18.verse: Sāriputta guides to the fruit of stream entry, monks, Moggallāna guides to the supreme good.

cbv28:1.1.19.verse: Sāriputta is able, monks, ° to explain, reveal, make known, set forth, open up, analyse, and make plain, the four noble truths in detail.”

cbv28:1.1.21.verse: and after saying this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went into his living quarters.

cbv28:1.1.22.verse: Then venerable Sāriputta, not long after the Fortunate One had gone, addressed the monks, saying:

cbv28:1.1.24.verse: “Venerable friend!” those monks replied to venerable Sāriputta,

cbv28:1.1.26.verse: “The Realised One, friends, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.27.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of the four noble truths.

cbv28:2.1.verse: The First Noble Truth and its Analysis

cbv28:3.1.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of suffering?

cbv28:3.1.2.verse: Birth is suffering also old age is suffering also sickness is suffering also death is suffering also grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, is suffering also not to obtain what one longs for is suffering in brief, the five constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment are suffering.

cbv28:3.1.3.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is birth?

cbv28:3.1.4.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is birth, being born, appearing, turning up;

cbv28:3.1.5.verse: the manifestation of the constituent groups (of mind and body), the acquisition of the sense spheres: this venerable friends, is called birth.

cbv28:3.1.6.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is old age?

cbv28:3.1.7.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is aging, agedness, broken teeth, greying hair, and wrinkled skin;

cbv28:3.1.8.verse: the dwindling away of the lifespan, the decay of the sense faculties: this venerable friends, is called old age.

cbv28:3.1.9.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is death?

cbv28:3.1.10.verse: For the various beings in the various classes of beings there is a fall, a falling away, a breaking up, a disappearance, a dying, a death, a making of time;

cbv28:3.1.11.verse: the break up of the constituent groups (of mind and body), the throwing off of the body, this, venerable friends, is called death.

cbv28:3.1.12.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is grief?

cbv28:3.1.13.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

cbv28:3.1.14.verse: there is grief, grieving, the state of grieving, inner grief, great inner grief: this, venerable friends, is called grief.

cbv28:3.1.15.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is lamenation?

cbv28:3.1.16.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

cbv28:3.1.17.verse: there are laments, great laments, lamenting, great lamenting, the state of lamenting, great lamentation: this, venerable friends, is called lamentation.

cbv28:3.1.18.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is pain?

cbv28:3.1.19.verse: That, venerable friends, which is bodily pain, bodily disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the body, disagreeable feeling:

cbv28:3.1.20.verse: this, venerable friends, is called pain.

cbv28:3.1.21.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is sorrow?

cbv28:3.1.22.verse: That, venerable friends, which is mental pain, mental disagreeableness, pain born of contact with the mind, disagreeable feeling:

cbv28:3.1.23.verse: this, venerable friends, is called sorrow.

cbv28:3.1.24.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is despair?

cbv28:3.1.25.verse: For he who has, venerable friends, some sort of misfortune or other, who is touched by some sort of pain or another,

cbv28:3.1.26.verse: there is desponding, despairing, despondency, despair: this, venerable friends, is called despair.

cbv28:3.1.27.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for?

cbv28:3.1.28.verse: To those beings subject to birth, venerable friends, this longing arises:

cbv28:3.1.29.verse: “Oh, might we not be subject to birth, and may birth surely not come to us!”

cbv28:3.1.30.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

cbv28:3.1.31.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

cbv28:4.1.verse: To those beings subject to old age, venerable friends, this longing arises:

cbv28:4.2.verse: “Oh, might we not be subject to old age,

cbv28:4.3.verse: may old age surely not come to us!”

cbv28:4.4.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

cbv28:4.5.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

cbv28:5.1.verse: To those beings subject to sickness, venerable friends, this longing arises:

cbv28:5.2.verse: “Oh, might we not be subject to sickness,

cbv28:5.3.verse: may old age surely not come to us!”

cbv28:5.4.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

cbv28:5.5.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

cbv28:6.1.verse: To those beings subject to death, venerable friends, this longing arises:

cbv28:6.2.verse: “Oh, might we not be subject to death,

cbv28:6.3.verse: may death surely not come to us!”

cbv28:6.4.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

cbv28:6.5.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

cbv28:7.1.1.verse: To those beings subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, venerable friends, this longing arises:

cbv28:7.1.2.verse: ° “Oh, might we not be subject to grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair, may grief, lamentation, pain, sorrow, and despair surely not come to us!”

cbv28:7.1.3.verse: But that cannot be attained merely by longing for it:

cbv28:7.1.4.verse: this is the suffering from not obtaining what one longs for.

cbv28:7.1.5.verse: Now what, venerable friends, in brief, are the constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment that are suffering?

cbv28:7.1.6.verse: They are as follows: the form constituent group that is attached to the feelings constituent group that is attached to the perceptions constituent group that is attached to the (mental) processes constituent group that is attached to the consciousness constituent group that is attached to.

cbv28:7.1.7.verse: These, venerable friends, in brief, are called the constituent groups (of mind and body) that provide fuel for attachment and that are suffering.

cbv28:7.1.8.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of suffering.

cbv28:9.1.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the arising of suffering?

cbv28:9.1.2.verse: It is that craving which leads to continuation in existence, which is connected with enjoyment and passion, greatly enjoying this and that, as follows:

cbv28:9.1.3.verse: craving for sense pleasures craving for continuation craving for discontinuation.

cbv28:9.1.4.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the arising of suffering.

cbv28:11.1.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

cbv28:11.1.2.verse: It is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that craving - liberation, letting go, release, and non-adherence.

cbv28:11.1.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:12.1.verse: The Fourth Noble Truth and its Analysis

cbv28:13.1.1.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering?

cbv28:13.1.2.verse: It is this noble path with eight factors, as follows:

cbv28:13.1.3.verse: right view right thought right speech right action right livelihood right endeavour right mindfulness right concentration.

cbv28:13.1.4.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right view?

cbv28:13.1.5.verse: That, venerable friends, which is knowledge about suffering knowledge about the arising of suffering knowledge about the cessation of suffering knowledge about the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:13.1.6.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right view.

cbv28:13.1.7.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right thought?

cbv28:13.1.8.verse: The thought of renunciation the thought of good will the thought of non-violence.

cbv28:13.1.9.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right thought.

cbv28:13.1.10.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right speech?

cbv28:13.1.11.verse: Refraining from false speech refraining from malicious speech refraining from rough speech refraining from frivolous talk.

cbv28:13.1.12.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right speech.

cbv28:13.1.13.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right action?

cbv28:13.1.14.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures refraining from taking what has not been given refraining from sexual misconduct.

cbv28:13.1.15.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right action.

cbv28:13.1.16.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right livelihood?

cbv28:13.1.17.verse: Here, venerable friends, a noble disciple, having given up wrong ways of livelihood, earns his living by a right way of livelihood.

cbv28:13.1.18.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right livelihood.

cbv28:13.1.19.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right endeavour?

cbv28:13.1.20.verse: ° Here, venerable friends, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of bad and unwholesome things that have not yet arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

cbv28:13.1.21.verse: ° He generates desire to give up bad and unwholesome things that have already arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

cbv28:13.1.22.verse: He generates desire for the arising of wholesome things that have not yet arisen, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

cbv28:13.1.23.verse: ° He generates desire for the endurance of wholesome things that have arisen, their non-forgetting, multiplicaton, extension, development, and fulfilment, (in this regard) he endeavours, instigates energy, exerts his mind, and makes an effort.

cbv28:13.1.24.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right endeavour.

cbv28:13.1.25.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right mindfulness?

cbv28:13.1.26.verse: Here, venerable friends, a monk dwells contemplating (the nature of) the body in the body, ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

cbv28:14.1.verse: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) feelings in feelings,

cbv28:14.2.verse: ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

cbv28:15.1.verse: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) the mind in the mind,

cbv28:15.2.verse: ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

cbv28:16.1.1.verse: He dwells contemplating (the nature of) things in (various) things ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world.

cbv28:16.1.2.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right mindfulness.

cbv28:16.1.3.verse: Now what, venerable friends, is right concentration?

cbv28:16.1.4.verse: Here, venerable friends, a monk, quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unwholesome things, having thinking, reflection, and the happiness and rapture born of seclusion, dwells having attained the first absorption.

cbv28:16.1.5.verse: With the ending of thinking, and reflection, with internal clarity, and one-pointedness of mind, being without thinking, without reflection, having the happiness and rapture born of concentration, he dwells having attained the second absorption.

cbv28:17.1.verse: With the fading away of rapture he dwells equanimous,

cbv28:17.2.verse: mindful, clearly knowing, experiencing happiness through the body,

cbv28:17.3.verse: about which the Noble Ones declare: “He lives pleasantly, mindful, and equanimous,”

cbv28:17.4.verse: (thus) he dwells having attained the third absorption.

cbv28:18.1.1.verse: he dwells having attained the fourth absorption.

cbv28:18.1.2.verse: This, venerable friends, is called right concentration.

cbv28:18.1.3.verse: This, venerable friends, is called the noble truth of the practice going to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:18.1.4.verse: The Realised One, friends, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel, and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:18.1.5.verse: ° That is to say, the explanation, revealing, making known, setting forth, opening up, analysing, and making plain, of these four noble truths.”

cbv28:18.1.7.verse: and those monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in venerable Sāriputta’s words.

cbv28:19.1.verse: The Seven Extra Discourses are Finished

cbv28:1.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Varanasi in the deer park at Isipatana.

cbv28:1.1.3.verse: There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,

cbv28:1.1.7.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.8.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

cbv28:1.1.10.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:1.1.11.verse: Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.12.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

cbv28:1.1.13.verse: Mendicants, you should cultivate friendship with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

cbv28:1.1.14.verse: You should associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

cbv28:1.1.15.verse: They’re astute, and they support their spiritual companions.

cbv28:1.1.16.verse: Sāriputta is like one who gives birth,

cbv28:1.1.17.verse: while Moggallāna is like one who raises the child.

cbv28:1.1.18.verse: Sāriputta guides people to the fruit of stream-entry, Moggallāna to the highest goal.

cbv28:1.1.19.verse: Sāriputta is able to explain, teach, assert, establish, clarify, analyze, and reveal the four noble truths in detail.”

cbv28:1.1.20.verse: That is what the Buddha said.

cbv28:1.1.21.verse: When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

cbv28:1.1.22.verse: Then, not long after the Buddha left, Venerable Sāriputta said to the mendicants,

cbv28:1.1.26.verse: “Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:1.1.27.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.

cbv28:1.1.29.verse: The noble truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:3.1.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of suffering?

cbv28:3.1.2.verse: Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.

cbv28:3.1.4.verse: The rebirth, inception, conception, regeneration, manifestation of the aggregates, and acquisition of the sense fields of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

cbv28:3.1.7.verse: The old age, decrepitude, broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkly skin, diminished vitality, and failing faculties of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

cbv28:3.1.10.verse: The passing away, passing on, disintegration, demise, mortality, death, decease, breaking up of the aggregates, laying to rest of the corpse, and cutting off of the life faculty of the various sentient beings in the various orders of sentient beings.

cbv28:3.1.13.verse: The sorrow, sorrowing, state of sorrow, inner sorrow, inner deep sorrow in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

cbv28:3.1.16.verse: The wail, lament, wailing, lamenting, state of wailing and lamentation in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

cbv28:3.1.19.verse: Physical pain, physical unpleasantness, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from physical contact.

cbv28:3.1.22.verse: Mental pain, mental displeasure, the painful, unpleasant feeling that’s born from mind contact.

cbv28:3.1.25.verse: The stress, distress, state of stress and distress in someone who has undergone misfortune, who has experienced suffering.

cbv28:3.1.27.verse: And what is ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’?

cbv28:3.1.28.verse: In sentient beings who are liable to be reborn, such a wish arises:

cbv28:3.1.29.verse: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to be reborn! If only rebirth would not come to us!’

cbv28:3.1.30.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

cbv28:3.1.31.verse: This is: ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

cbv28:7.1.1.verse: experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, such a wish arises:

cbv28:7.1.2.verse: ‘Oh, if only we were not liable to experience sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress! If only sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress would not come to us!’

cbv28:7.1.3.verse: But you can’t get that by wishing.

cbv28:7.1.4.verse: This is: ‘not getting what you wish for is suffering’.

cbv28:7.1.5.verse: And what is ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’?

cbv28:7.1.6.verse: They are the grasping aggregates that consist of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness.

cbv28:7.1.7.verse: This is called ‘in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering’.

cbv28:7.1.8.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

cbv28:9.1.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

cbv28:9.1.2.verse: It’s the craving that leads to future lives, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure there wherever it alights. That is,

cbv28:9.1.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for continued existence, and craving for nonexistence.

cbv28:9.1.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

cbv28:11.1.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

cbv28:11.1.2.verse: It’s the fading away and cessation of that very same craving no residue left behind; giving it away, letting it go, releasing it, and not clinging to it.

cbv28:11.1.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:13.1.1.verse: And what is the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?

cbv28:13.1.2.verse: It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:

cbv28:13.1.3.verse: right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

cbv28:13.1.5.verse: Knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:13.1.8.verse: Purposes of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness.

cbv28:13.1.11.verse: Refraining from lying, backbiting, harsh speech, and talking nonsense.

cbv28:13.1.14.verse: Refraining from killing living creatures, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

cbv28:13.1.17.verse: It’s when a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and earns a living by right livelihood.

cbv28:13.1.20.verse: It’s when a mendicant generates enthusiasm, tries, makes an effort, exerts the mind, and strives so that bad, unskillful qualities don’t arise.

cbv28:13.1.21.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen are given up.

cbv28:13.1.22.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities arise.

cbv28:13.1.23.verse: They generate enthusiasm, try, make an effort, exert the mind, and strive so that skillful qualities that have arisen remain, are not lost, but increase, mature, and are fully developed.

cbv28:13.1.26.verse: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

cbv28:16.1.1.verse: principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

cbv28:16.1.4.verse: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

cbv28:16.1.5.verse: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

cbv28:18.1.1.verse: With the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, they enter and remain in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

cbv28:18.1.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:18.1.4.verse: Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Isipatana, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha rolled forth the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. And that wheel cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.

cbv28:18.1.5.verse: It is the teaching, advocating, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing of the four noble truths.”

cbv28:18.1.6.verse: That is what Venerable Sāriputta said.

cbv28:18.1.7.verse: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what Sāriputta said.

cbv28:1.1.2.verse: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Benares in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

cbv28:1.1.3.verse: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:

cbv28:1.1.7.verse: “At Benares, bhikkhus, in the Deer Park at Isipatana the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, set rolling the matchless Wheel of the Dhamma, which cannot be stopped by any recluse or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world—that is,

cbv28:1.1.8.verse: the announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, expounding, and exhibiting of the Four Noble Truths.

cbv28:1.1.10.verse: “the announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, expounding, and exhibiting of the noble truth of suffering. the announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, expounding, and exhibiting of the noble truth of the origin of suffering…of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering…of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:1.1.11.verse: “At Benares, bhikkhus, in the Deer Park at Isipatana the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, set rolling the matchless Wheel of the Dhamma, which cannot be stopped by any recluse or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world—that is,

cbv28:1.1.12.verse: the announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, expounding, and exhibiting of these Four Noble Truths.

cbv28:1.1.13.verse: “Cultivate the friendship of Sāriputta and Moggallāna, bhikkhus;

cbv28:1.1.15.verse: They are wise and helpful to their companions in the holy life.

cbv28:1.1.18.verse: Sāriputta trains others for the fruit of stream-entry, Moggallāna for the supreme goal.

cbv28:1.1.19.verse: Sāriputta, bhikkhus, is able to announce, teach, describe, establish, reveal, expound, and exhibit the Four Noble Truths.”

cbv28:1.1.21.verse: Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling.

cbv28:1.1.22.verse: Then, soon after the Blessed One had gone, the venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus thus:

cbv28:1.1.24.verse: “Friend,” the bhikkhus replied to the venerable Sāriputta.

cbv28:1.1.26.verse: “At Benares, friends, in the Deer Park at Isipatana the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, set rolling the matchless Wheel of the Dhamma…

cbv28:1.1.27.verse: and exhibiting of the Four Noble Truths.

cbv28:1.1.29.verse: “The announcing…and exhibiting of the noble truth of suffering…of the noble truth of the origin of suffering…of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering…of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:3.1.1.verse: “And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering?

cbv28:3.1.2.verse: Birth is suffering; ageing is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to obtain what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering.

cbv28:3.1.4.verse: The birth of beings into the various orders of beings, their coming to birth, precipitation [in a womb], generation, the manifestation of the aggregates, obtaining the bases for contact—

cbv28:3.1.7.verse: The ageing of beings in the various orders of beings, their old age, brokenness of teeth, greyness of hair, wrinkling of skin, decline of life, weakness of faculties—

cbv28:3.1.10.verse: The passing of beings out of the various orders of beings, their passing away, dissolution, disappearance, dying, completion of time, dissolution of aggregates, laying down of the body—

cbv28:3.1.13.verse: The sorrow, sorrowing, sorrowfulness, inner sorrow, inner sorriness, of one who has encountered some misfortune or is affected by some painful state—

cbv28:3.1.16.verse: The wail and lament, wailing and lamenting, bewailing and lamentation, of one who has encountered some misfortune or is affected by some painful state—

cbv28:3.1.19.verse: Bodily pain, bodily discomfort, painful, uncomfortable feeling born of bodily contact—

cbv28:3.1.22.verse: Mental pain, mental discomfort, painful, uncomfortable feeling born of mental contact—

cbv28:3.1.25.verse: The trouble and despair, the tribulation and desperation, of one who has encountered some misfortune or is affected by some painful state—

cbv28:3.1.27.verse: “And what, friends, is ‘not to obtain what one wants is suffering’?

cbv28:3.1.28.verse: To beings subject to birth there comes the wish:

cbv28:3.1.29.verse: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to birth! That birth would not come to us!’

cbv28:3.1.30.verse: But this is not to be obtained by wishing,

cbv28:3.1.31.verse: and not to obtain what one wants is suffering.

cbv28:7.1.1.verse: subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, there comes the wish:

cbv28:7.1.2.verse: ‘Oh, that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair! That sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not come to us!’

cbv28:7.1.3.verse: But this is not to be obtained by wishing,

cbv28:7.1.4.verse: and not to obtain what one wants is suffering.

cbv28:7.1.5.verse: “And what, friends, are the five aggregates affected by clinging that, in short, are suffering?

cbv28:7.1.6.verse: They are: the material form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, and the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging.

cbv28:7.1.7.verse: These are the five aggregates affected by clinging that, in short, are suffering.

cbv28:7.1.8.verse: This is called the noble truth of suffering.

cbv28:9.1.1.verse: “And what, friends, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

cbv28:9.1.2.verse: It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is,

cbv28:9.1.3.verse: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for being, and craving for non-being.

cbv28:9.1.4.verse: This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

cbv28:11.1.1.verse: “And what, friends, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

cbv28:11.1.2.verse: It is the remainderless fading away and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go, and rejecting of that same craving.

cbv28:11.1.3.verse: This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:13.1.1.verse: “And what, friends, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering?

cbv28:13.1.2.verse: It is just this Noble Eightfold Path; that is,

cbv28:13.1.3.verse: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

cbv28:13.1.5.verse: Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—

cbv28:13.1.8.verse: Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, and intention of non-cruelty—

cbv28:13.1.11.verse: Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter—

cbv28:13.1.14.verse: Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from misconduct in sensual pleasures—

cbv28:13.1.17.verse: Here a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood—

cbv28:13.1.20.verse: Here a bhikkhu awakens zeal for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.

cbv28:13.1.21.verse: He awakens zeal for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.

cbv28:13.1.22.verse: He awakens zeal for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.

cbv28:13.1.23.verse: He awakens zeal for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, and fulfilment by development of arisen wholesome states, and he makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives.

cbv28:13.1.26.verse: Here a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

cbv28:16.1.1.verse: He abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.

cbv28:16.1.4.verse: Here, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

cbv28:16.1.5.verse: With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.

cbv28:18.1.1.verse: With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

cbv28:18.1.3.verse: “This is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

cbv28:18.1.4.verse: “At Benares, friends, in the Deer Park at Isipatana the Tathāgata, accomplished and fully enlightened, set rolling the matchless Wheel of the Dhamma, which cannot be stopped by any recluse or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world—that is,

cbv28:18.1.5.verse: the announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, expounding, and exhibiting of these Four Noble Truths.”

cbv28:18.1.6.verse: That is what the venerable Sāriputta said.

cbv28:18.1.7.verse: The bhikkhus were satisfied and delighted in the venerable Sāriputta’s words.

cbv29a:3.1.2.verse: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Rājagaha on the Vultures’ Peak mountain.

cbv29a:3.1.3.verse: Then the Four Great Kings, with a great army of yakkhas, with a great army of gandhabbas, with a great army of kumbhaṇḍas, with a great army of nāgas, having set up a protection over the four quarters, having set serried troops at the four directions, having set up a barricade at the four directions, at the end of the night, having lit up the whole of Vultures’ Peak with their surpassing beauty, approached the Fortunate One, and after approaching and worshipping the Fortunate One, they sat down on one side.

cbv29a:3.1.4.verse: Then of those yakkhas, some, after worshipping the Fortunate One, sat down on one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Fortunate One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down on one side. Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to the Fortunate One, sat down on one side. Some, after announcing their name and family, sat down on one side. Some, while keeping silent, sat down on one side.

cbv29a:3.1.5.verse: Then, while sitting on one side, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to the Fortunate One:

cbv29a:3.1.6.verse: “There are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29a:3.1.7.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29a:3.1.8.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29a:3.1.9.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29a:3.1.10.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29a:3.1.11.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One.

cbv29a:3.1.12.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas are not pleased with the Fortunate One.

cbv29a:3.1.13.verse: What is the reason for that?

cbv29a:3.1.14.verse: Because, reverend Sir, the Fortunate One preaches the Dhamma of refraining from killing living creatures, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from taking what has not been given, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from sexual misconduct, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from false speech, preaches the Dhamma of refraining from liquor, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

cbv29a:3.1.15.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas do not refrain from killing living creatures, do not refrain from taking what has not been given, do not refrain from sexual misconduct, do not refrain from false speech, do not refrain from liquors, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

cbv29a:3.1.16.verse: To them that is neither dear nor appealing.

cbv29a:3.1.17.verse: There are, reverend Sir, disciples of the Fortunate One in the wilderness, who are practising in remote jungle dwelling places, where there is little sound, little noise, which have a lonely atmosphere, lying hidden away from men, which are suitable for seclusion.

cbv29a:3.1.19.verse: To please then, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One learn this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.”

cbv29a:3.1.20.verse: The Fortunate One by keeping silent gave consent.

cbv29a:3.1.21.verse: Then the Great King Vessavaṇa having understood the Fortunate One’s consent on that occasion recited this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection:

cbv29a:13.1.91.verse: This, dear Sir, is the “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.

cbv29a:13.1.92.verse: Whoever, dear Sir - be they monk or nun or layman or laywoman - learns this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection well, and will master it in its entirety,

cbv29a:13.1.93.verse: then if a non-human being - be they male yakkha or female yakkha or yakkha boy or yakkha girl or yakkha minister or yakkha councillor or yakkha messenger or male gandhabba or female gandhabba or gandhabba boy or gandhabba girl or gandhabba minister or gandhabba councillor or gandhabba messenger or male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍa or kumbhaṇḍa boy or kumbhaṇḍa girl or kumbhaṇḍa minister or kumbhaṇḍa councillor or kumbhaṇḍa messenger or male nāga or female nāga or nāga boy or nāga girl or nāga minister or nāga councillor or nāga messenger - with a wicked mind come near while they are going, or stand near while they are standing, or sit near while they are sitting, or lie near while they are lying,

cbv29a:13.1.94.verse: then that non-human being, dear Sir, would not receive in my villages and towns, honour or respect.

cbv29a:13.1.95.verse: That non-human being, dear Sir, would not receive in my royal city Ālakamandā, ground or dwelling.

cbv29a:13.1.96.verse: That non-human being, dear Sir, would not be able to go to the gathering of the yakkhas.

cbv29a:13.1.97.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would not give or take him in marriage.

cbv29a:13.1.98.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would abuse him with very personal abuse.

cbv29a:13.1.99.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would drop an empty bowl over his head.

cbv29a:13.1.100.verse: Further, dear Sir, non-human beings would split his head into seven pieces.

cbv29a:13.1.101.verse: There are non-human beings, dear Sir, who are fierce, cruel, and violent, they do not take notice of the Great Kings, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ men, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ mens’ men,

cbv29a:13.1.102.verse: and those non-human beings, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the Great Kings.

cbv29a:13.1.103.verse: Just as, dear Sir, there are thieves in the king of Magadha’s realm,

cbv29a:13.1.104.verse: who do not take notice of the king of Magadha, who do not take notice of the king of Magadha’s men, who do not take notice of the king of Magadha’s mens’ men,

cbv29a:13.1.105.verse: and those great thieves, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the king of Magadha.

cbv29a:13.1.106.verse: Even so, dear Sir, there are non-human beings who are fierce, cruel, and violent, they do not take notice of the Great Kings, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ men, they do not take notice of the Great Kings’ mens’ men,

cbv29a:13.1.107.verse: and those non-human beings, dear Sir, are said to be in revolt against the Great Kings.

cbv29a:13.1.108.verse: Now, dear Sir, whatever non-human beings - be they male yakkha or female yakkha or yakkha boy or yakkha girl or yakkha minister or yakkha councillor or yakkha messenger or male gandhabba or female gandhabba or gandhabba boy or gandhabba girl or gandhabba minister or gandhabba councillor or gandhabba messenger or male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍa or kumbhaṇḍa boy or kumbhaṇḍa girl or kumbhaṇḍa minister or kumbhaṇḍa councillor or kumbhaṇḍa messenger or male nāga or female nāga or nāga boy or nāga girl or nāga minister or nāga councillor or nāga messenger - with a wicked mind should come near a monk or a nun or a layman or a laywoman while they are going, or stand near while they are standing, or sit near while they are sitting, or lie near while they are lying,

cbv29a:13.1.109.verse: then to these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, great generals, one should call out, one should shout out, one should cry out:

cbv29a:13.1.110.verse: “This yakkha has seized me, this yakkha has grabbed me, this yakkha annoys me, this yakkha harasses me, this yakkha hurts me, this yakkha injures me, this yakkha will not release me.”

cbv29a:13.1.111.verse: To which yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals?

cbv29a:13.1.130.verse: then to these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals, one should call out, one should shout out, one should cry out:

cbv29a:13.1.131.verse: “This yakkha has seized me, this yakkha has grabbed me, this yakkha annoys me, this yakkha harasses me, this yakkha hurts me, this yakkha injures me, this yakkha will not release me.”

cbv29a:13.1.132.verse: This, dear Sir, is the “Āṭānāṭiyā” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.

cbv29a:13.1.133.verse: And now, dear Sir, we shall go, as we have many duties, and there is much which ought to be done.”

cbv29a:13.1.134.verse: “Now is the time for whatever you Great Kings are thinking.”

cbv29a:13.1.135.verse: ° Then the Four Great Kings rose from their seats and after worshipping and circumambulating the Fortunate One, vanished right there.

cbv29a:13.1.136.verse: ° Then some yakkhas rose from their seats and after worshipping and circumambulating the Fortunate One, vanished right there. ° Some exchanged greetings with the Fortunate One, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, vanished right there. ° Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to the Fortunate One, vanished right there. Some, after announcing their name and family vanished right there. And some, while keeping silent, vanished right there.

cbv29a:3.1.2.verse: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

cbv29a:3.1.3.verse: Then, late at night, the four great kings—with large armies of spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—set guards, troops, and wards at the four quarters and then, lighting up the entire Vulture’s Peak with their beauty, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

cbv29a:3.1.4.verse: Before sitting down to one side, some spirits bowed, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

cbv29a:3.1.5.verse: Seated to one side, the Great King Vessavaṇa said to the Buddha,

cbv29a:3.1.6.verse: “Sir, some high spirits have confidence in the Buddha,

cbv29a:3.1.8.verse: Some middling spirits have confidence in the Buddha,

cbv29a:3.1.10.verse: Some low spirits have confidence in the Buddha,

cbv29a:3.1.12.verse: But mostly the spirits don’t have confidence in the Buddha.

cbv29a:3.1.14.verse: Because the Buddha teaches them to refrain from killing living creatures, stealing, lying, sexual misconduct, and consuming intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.

cbv29a:3.1.15.verse: But mostly they don’t refrain from such things.

cbv29a:3.1.16.verse: They don’t like that or approve of it.

cbv29a:3.1.17.verse: Sir, there are disciples of the Buddha who frequent remote lodgings in the wilderness and the forest that are quiet and still, far from the madding crowd, remote from human settlements, and fit for retreat.

cbv29a:3.1.18.verse: There dwell high spirits who have no confidence in the Buddha’s dispensation.

cbv29a:3.1.19.verse: To give them confidence, may the Buddha please learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”

cbv29a:3.1.21.verse: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, on that occasion Great King Vessavaṇa recited the Āṭānāṭiya protection.

cbv29a:13.1.92.verse: The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen should learn this Āṭānāṭiya protection well and completely memorize it.

cbv29a:13.1.93.verse: If anyone who does so is approached while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down by any non-human being with malicious intent—including males, females, boys, girls, chief ministers, councillors, and servants among the spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—

cbv29a:13.1.94.verse: that non-human will receive no homage or respect in any village or town.

cbv29a:13.1.95.verse: And they will receive no ground or dwelling in my capital of Ālakamandā.

cbv29a:13.1.96.verse: Nor will they get to go to the conference of the spirits.

cbv29a:13.1.97.verse: In addition, the non-humans would not give or take them in marriage.

cbv29a:13.1.98.verse: They’d heap personal abuse on them,

cbv29a:13.1.99.verse: drop an empty bowl on their head,

cbv29a:13.1.100.verse: and even split their head into seven pieces!

cbv29a:13.1.101.verse: For there are, good fellow, non-humans who are fierce, cruel, and violent. They don’t obey the Great Kings or their men or their men’s men.

cbv29a:13.1.102.verse: They’re said to be rebelling against the Great Kings.

cbv29a:13.1.103.verse: They’re just like the bandits in the king of Magadha’s realm

cbv29a:13.1.104.verse: who don’t obey the king, his men, or his men’s men,

cbv29a:13.1.105.verse: and are said to be rebelling against the king.

cbv29a:13.1.108.verse: If any non-human being with malicious intent—including males, females, boys, girls, ministers, councillors, and servants among the spirits, centaurs, gnomes, and dragons—approaches a monk, nun, layman, or laywoman while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,

cbv29a:13.1.109.verse: one ought to yell, cry, and scream to the spirits, great spirits, generals, great generals:

cbv29a:13.1.110.verse: ‘This spirit’s got me! This spirit’s entered me! This spirit’s annoying me! This spirit’s harassing me! This spirit’s hurting me! This spirit’s harming me! This spirit won’t let me go!’

cbv29a:13.1.111.verse: To what spirits, great spirits, generals, great generals?

cbv29a:13.1.119.verse: and the kings Nala and Janesabha,

cbv29a:13.1.132.verse: This, good fellow, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, safety, and comfort of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

cbv29a:13.1.133.verse: Well, now, good fellow, I must go. I have many duties, and much to do.”

cbv29a:13.1.134.verse: “Please, Great Kings, go at your convenience.”

cbv29a:13.1.135.verse: Then the four great kings got up from their seats, bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, before vanishing right there.

cbv29a:13.1.136.verse: And before the other spirits present vanished, some bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right side, some exchanged greetings and polite conversation, some held up their cupped palms toward the Buddha, some announced their name and clan, while some kept silent.

cbv29b:2.1.1.verse: Then the Fortunate One when that night had passed addressed the monks, saying:

cbv29b:2.1.2.verse: “This night, monks, the Four Great Kings, with a great army of yakkhas, with a great army of gandhabbas, with a great army of kumbhaṇḍas, with a great army of nāgas, having set up a protection over the four quarters, having set serried troops at the four directions, having set up a barricade at the four directions, at the end of the night, having lit up the whole of Vultures’ Peak with their surpassing beauty, approached me, and after approaching and worshipping me, they sat down on one side.

cbv29b:2.1.3.verse: Then of those yakkhas, monks, some, after worshipping me, sat down on one side. Some exchanged greetings with me, and after exchanging polite and courteous greetings, sat down on one side. Some, after raising their hands in respectful salutation to me, sat down on one side. Some, after announcing their name and family, sat down on one side. Some, while keeping silent, sat down on one side.

cbv29b:2.1.4.verse: Then, while sitting on one side, monks, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to me:

cbv29b:3.1.verse: “There are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29b:3.2.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some high ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29b:3.3.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29b:3.4.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some middle ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29b:3.5.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are not pleased with the Fortunate One,

cbv29b:3.6.verse: there are, reverend Sir, some low ranking yakkhas who are pleased with the Fortunate One.

cbv29b:4.1.1.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas are not pleased with the Fortunate One.

cbv29b:4.1.2.verse: What is the reason for that?

cbv29b:5.1.verse: Because, reverend Sir, the Fortunate One preaches the Dhamma of refraining from killing living creatures,

cbv29b:5.2.verse: preaches the Dhamma of refraining from taking what has not been given,

cbv29b:5.3.verse: preaches the Dhamma of refraining from sexual misconduct,

cbv29b:5.4.verse: preaches the Dhamma of refraining from false speech,

cbv29b:5.5.verse: preaches the Dhamma of refraining from liquor, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

cbv29b:5.6.verse: But, reverend Sir, almost all of the yakkhas do not refrain from killing living creatures,

cbv29b:5.7.verse: do not refrain from taking what has not been given,

cbv29b:5.8.verse: do not refrain from sexual misconduct,

cbv29b:5.9.verse: do not refrain from false speech,

cbv29b:5.10.verse: do not refrain from liquors, wines, or intoxicants which cause heedlessness.

cbv29b:6.1.1.verse: To them that is neither dear nor appealing.

cbv29b:6.1.2.verse: There are, reverend Sir, disciples of the Fortunate One in the wilderness, who are practising in remote jungle dwelling places, where there is little sound, little noise, which have a lonely atmosphere, lying hidden away from men, which are suitable for seclusion.

cbv29b:6.1.3.verse: And there are high ranking yakkhas settled there who are not pleased with the word of the Fortunate One, To please then, reverend Sir, may the Fortunate One learn this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection, for the monks’, nuns’, laymen’s, and laywomen’s guard, protection, freedom from harm, and comfortable living.”

cbv29b:6.1.4.verse: And I, monks, by keeping silent, gave consent.

cbv29b:6.1.5.verse: Then the Great King Vessavaṇa, monks, having understood my consent on that occasion recited this “Āṭānāṭiya” protection:
